hook: Your photos live happily as objects. Why would the database behind them refuse the same deal?
title: Databases don't want objects. They want a disk.
body:
An object store hands back whole, immutable objects by key. That is perfect for photos and useless for a database. The profile store, the message store and the search index need to overwrite small pieces of data at any offset, thousands of times per second, with sub-millisecond latency.

They also need one promise: a write is safe once `fsync` returns. Random overwrites plus that durability guarantee is exactly what **block storage** sells: a long array of fixed-size blocks you can rewrite in place.
takeaway: Objects are for things you replace. Blocks are for things you rewrite.
deeper:
**Why objects fail here:** Changing one byte of an immutable object means writing a new object. A database commits thousands of tiny changes per second, each touching a few KiB somewhere in a large file. Rewriting whole objects for that makes no sense.

**What the database needs:** Three things at once. Random reads and overwrites at any offset. Latency under a millisecond, because commit time waits on storage. And a clear durability point: once `fsync` returns, the write survives a crash.

**Where this leads:** Clouds deliver this as network volumes, such as AWS EBS, Google Persistent Disk and Azure Managed Disks, or as local NVMe flash inside the host. Choosing between them, and making sure `fsync` really means safe, is most of what running a database's storage is about. Kubernetes adds a final twist: handing disks to a system originally built for stateless pods.

quiz.q: Your team proposes storing a message database's pages as objects in an object store, one object per page. What breaks first?
quiz.a: Every small update would rewrite a whole immutable object. The database needs in-place overwrites at any offset, thousands per second, at sub-millisecond latency, with a clear fsync durability point.

mcq.q: What does a database need from storage that an object store does not offer?
options: In-place overwrites at any offset, sub-millisecond
Higher durability than eleven nines
Immutable copies of every past version
Lookup of whole files by a key
mcq.why: Databases rewrite small blocks thousands of times per second and need low latency plus an fsync durability point. Objects are whole and immutable.

hook: Your disk has no idea what a file is.
title: A block device knows numbers, not names
body:
Strip away the filesystem and a disk is almost nothing. A **block device** is a flat array of fixed-size blocks, usually 512 bytes or 4 KiB. It understands three verbs: read N blocks at offset X, write N blocks at offset X, and flush.

No filenames, no directories, no permissions. All of that is built on top, by a filesystem like ext4 or XFS, or by a database engine that manages the blocks itself.
takeaway: The disk stores numbered blocks. Meaning is always someone else's job.
deeper:
**Why so little:** Because the device promises nothing beyond numbered blocks, every higher layer can impose its own layout. A filesystem builds files, directories and a journal. A database keeps its own page format, buffer pool and write-ahead log.

**The verb that matters:** Reads and writes may be buffered along the way. Flush is how a caller demands that earlier writes reach stable storage. A database only cares that when it writes a block and flushes, that block is durable.

**Size has a cost:** With 4 KiB blocks, even a 1-byte change rewrites at least 4 KiB. Databases typically do random reads of 8-16 KiB, which is why their workloads are quoted in those sizes.

**The catch:** The device cannot tell which blocks form a complete file. That is why a block-level snapshot, taken without help from the layers above, is only crash-consistent.

quiz.q: A tool copies every block of a volume at one instant. Why can't it promise that each file inside the copy is complete?
quiz.a: The block device has no notion of files. Structure lives in the filesystem or database above it, so the device can't know which blocks belong together or which writes are still pending.

mcq.q: Which operations does a raw block device support?
options: Read blocks, write blocks, flush
Open, read, write and close files
Put, get and delete objects by key
Create, rename and delete directories
mcq.why: A block device is a flat array of fixed-size blocks. Files, names and directories come from the filesystem or database built on top.

hook: Your VM's disk shows up as /dev/nvme1n1, but the blocks sit on other servers. Why is that a feature?
title: Your cloud disk is a network service in disguise
body:
In the cloud, the disk your VM sees is a **volume**: a virtual block device. It looks exactly like a local disk, but the blocks live on storage servers across the network.

That hop costs latency on every I/O. What you get back is independence. The volume's life is separate from the VM's. You can detach it, attach it to another VM, snapshot it and resize it. When the VM dies, the data doesn't.
takeaway: Put the disk on the network and the data outlives the machine.
deeper:
**Why it matters:** If a VM fails, its volume is still intact on the storage servers. You attach it to a replacement, often within minutes, and carry on. You can grow capacity without changing instance type, and snapshot for backups.

**The price:** Every I/O crosses the network, so latency is hundreds of microseconds instead of the tens you get from flash inside the host. The volume also depends on a whole distributed storage system with its own failure modes, from noisy neighbors to control-plane outages.

**How far the disguise goes:** On AWS Nitro instances, a remote EBS volume appears to the guest as an NVMe device. A dedicated Nitro card handles the network protocol, encryption and I/O processing. The operating system simply sees and drives an ordinary NVMe device.

**The contrast:** Local NVMe instance storage skips the hop and is much faster, but its data is lost when the instance stops.

quiz.q: Two VMs are terminated: one used a network volume, the other instance-store NVMe. Which data can you bring back in minutes, and how?
quiz.a: The network volume's. Its lifecycle is independent of the VM, so you attach it to a new VM. Instance-store data is lost when the instance terminates.

mcq.q: What does separating a cloud volume's lifecycle from the VM let you do?
options: Detach it and attach it to another VM
Survive the loss of its whole zone
Skip the network hop on every I/O
Stop needing snapshots or replicas
mcq.why: The volume lives on storage servers, not in the VM, so it can be detached, reattached, snapshotted and resized independently.

hook: Two teams both say "the disk is slow". One means commits, the other means backups. Same fix?
title: Every volume has three speeds, and they're not the same
body:
"The disk is slow" hides three different problems. **IOPS** counts separate reads and writes per second; databases doing random 8-16 KiB reads live on it. **Throughput** counts bytes per second in MiB/s; log scans and backups live on it. **Latency** is how long one I/O takes, and transaction commit time depends on it directly.

A backup can max out throughput at modest IOPS. A commit path can crawl on a volume with IOPS to spare. Find the limit before you buy.
takeaway: "The disk is slow" is not a diagnosis until you name the number.
deeper:
**They are linked:** Throughput = IOPS × I/O size, so one volume can look IOPS-bound for small I/Os and throughput-bound for large ones. Little's Law adds the other link: IOPS = queue depth / latency. Latency quietly caps IOPS for any app that doesn't keep many I/Os in flight.

**Matching work to metric:**
1. Random point lookups in a database: IOPS and latency.
2. A backup or sequential log scan: throughput, with little care for per-I/O latency.
3. A commit path: waits on at least one storage round trip, so latency.

**The catch:** Cloud products advertise maximums. A 64,000-IOPS volume only delivers that to a workload parallel enough to ask for it. The first useful question on any slow-disk ticket is which of the three numbers is actually at its limit, and whether the workload can even reach it.

quiz.q: Backups still run fine, but commits got slower after moving a database to a volume with double the IOPS and a longer network path. What changed?
quiz.a: Latency. Each commit waits on at least one storage round trip, so a slower path hurts commits. Extra IOPS don't help, and backups care about throughput, not per-I/O latency.

mcq.q: Which metric most directly sets transaction commit time?
options: Latency of a single I/O
Provisioned IOPS ceiling
Maximum throughput in MiB/s
Volume capacity in GiB
mcq.why: Each commit waits for at least one storage round trip to finish, so per-I/O latency sets commit time.

hook: Same volume, two jobs. One tops out near 1,000 IOPS, the other at 16,000. Neither is broken.

predict.q: A volume allows 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s. A backup streams 1 MiB I/Os. What limits it?
options: Throughput, at about 1,000 IOPS
IOPS, at 16,000 operations
Neither; it gets both maximums

title: Big I/Os hit the MiB/s cap. Small ones hit IOPS.
body:
Every volume has two caps, and one formula decides which you hit: throughput = IOPS × I/O size. Take a volume capped at 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s.

A backup streaming 1 MiB chunks reaches 1,000 MiB/s at only about 1,000 IOPS. A database doing random 8 KiB reads hits 16,000 IOPS while moving about 125 MiB/s. The crossover sits near 64 KiB per I/O. Larger I/Os run out of bytes first. Smaller ones run out of operations.
takeaway: Know your I/O size before you read the spec sheet.
deeper:
**The crossover:** 1,000 MiB/s ÷ 16,000 IOPS ≈ 64 KiB. Above that size the throughput cap binds; below it the IOPS cap binds.

**Waste both ways:** The 8 KiB database uses one eighth of the throughput it pays for. The 1 MiB backup uses one sixteenth of its IOPS budget. Forcing every workload to buy both dimensions together wastes money on whichever one it doesn't touch.

**Why clouds changed pricing:** Newer types, such as AWS gp3 and io2, Azure Premium SSD v2 and Google Hyperdisk, avoid that waste by letting you provision IOPS and throughput separately.

**Read the fine print:** AWS quotes its HDD types, st1 and sc1, at 500 and 250 IOPS measured with 1 MiB I/Os. Spinning disks are built for big sequential transfers, and the spec reflects that. When sizing, start from the workload's typical I/O size, then check both caps.

quiz.q: A log-scan job moves from 16 KiB reads to 256 KiB reads on the same 16,000 IOPS / 1,000 MiB/s volume. Which cap limits it now?
quiz.a: Throughput. Above roughly 64 KiB per I/O, 1,000 MiB/s is reached before 16,000 IOPS. At 256 KiB that happens at about 4,000 IOPS.

mcq.q: A volume allows 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s. Random 8 KiB reads at full IOPS move roughly how much data?
options: About 125 MiB/s
About 1,000 MiB/s
About 64 MiB/s
About 500 MiB/s
mcq.why: 16,000 × 8 KiB = 128,000 KiB/s, about 125 MiB/s. Small I/Os exhaust the IOPS cap long before the throughput cap.

hook: Why does a single-threaded app get 2,000 IOPS from a volume rated for 64,000?
title: One thread can't spend the IOPS you paid for
body:
Provisioned IOPS is a ceiling, not a speed. **Little's Law** decides what you actually get: IOPS = queue depth / latency, where **queue depth** is the number of I/Os in flight.

At 0.5 ms latency with one outstanding I/O, the maximum is 1 / 0.0005 = 2,000 IOPS, whatever you provisioned. Reaching 64,000 IOPS at 0.5 ms needs about 32 I/Os in flight at once. A single-threaded app never gets there.

stat.label: IOPS ceiling: 0.5 ms latency, one I/O in flight

takeaway: Latency sets the speed limit. Concurrency decides how many lanes you use.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:**
1. One I/O takes 0.5 ms, so one at a time gives 2,000 per second.
2. 64,000 × 0.0005 = 32, so the full rating needs 32 in flight.
3. Latency is a property of the storage path, including the network hop, and is largely fixed for a given product.

**The only levers:** At fixed latency, you multiply IOPS with concurrency: many threads issuing synchronous I/O, or asynchronous I/O that keeps many requests outstanding. Or you lower latency with faster storage.

**It shows up in databases:** A single commit stream waiting on one `fsync` at a time over a 0.5 ms path cannot exceed about 2,000 commits per second. That is why databases batch commits.

**The habit:** When a benchmark shows a fraction of the rated IOPS, check queue depth before blaming the storage.

quiz.q: Storage latency drops from 0.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Your single-threaded app still keeps one I/O in flight. What is its new IOPS ceiling?
quiz.a: About 10,000 IOPS. By Little's Law, 1 / 0.0001 = 10,000. Lower latency raises the ceiling for the same queue depth.

mcq.q: How many I/Os must be in flight to reach 64,000 IOPS at 0.5 ms latency?
options: About 32
About 2
About 128
About 640
mcq.why: Queue depth = IOPS × latency = 64,000 × 0.0005 = 32.

hook: Your app is slow, so you triple the provisioned IOPS. The dashboard doesn't move. What did you buy?

predict.q: A single-threaded app doing one synchronous I/O at a time gets 2,000 IOPS. You triple provisioned IOPS. What does it get?
options: Still about 2,000 IOPS
About 6,000 IOPS
About 4,000 IOPS

title: More IOPS won't fix an app that waits on each I/O
body:
The IOPS number is the most visible knob on a cloud volume, and raising it is one API call. That makes it the favorite wrong fix.

If the app issues one synchronous I/O at a time, it is bound by latency, not by the ceiling. At 0.5 ms per I/O it tops out near 2,000 IOPS whether the volume allows 16,000 or 64,000. The real fixes are more I/Os in flight, or lower-latency storage such as local NVMe.
takeaway: If queue depth is one, the IOPS setting is not your problem.
deeper:
**Why it's predictable:** Little's Law says IOPS = queue depth / latency. With queue depth one, the provisioned figure never enters the equation. The volume reports the same 2,000 IOPS because the app never asks for more.

**Fix 1, concurrency:** More worker threads, asynchronous I/O or batching raise the number of I/Os in flight, so the ceiling you paid for becomes reachable.

**Fix 2, latency:** Local NVMe answers in tens of microseconds instead of hundreds. Same queue depth, much higher ceiling.

**Databases use both:** Group commit batches many transactions into one `fsync`. Some companies move latency-sensitive databases onto local disks; PlanetScale reported up to a 65% drop in p99 query latency for workloads that moved.

**The diagnostic:** Measure observed latency and queue depth first. Spend money only on the limit you're actually hitting.

quiz.q: A batch job does one synchronous 8 KiB read at a time from a volume with 0.5 ms latency. Name two changes that would actually speed it up.
quiz.a: Issue many reads concurrently (more threads, async I/O or batching), or move to lower-latency storage such as local NVMe. Raising provisioned IOPS alone changes nothing.

mcq.q: Which change speeds up a latency-bound app issuing one I/O at a time?
options: Keeping more I/Os in flight at once
Raising the provisioned IOPS cap
Raising the provisioned throughput cap
Buying a larger volume for more IOPS
mcq.why: With queue depth one, IOPS = 1 / latency. Only more concurrency or lower latency raises it; bigger caps go unused.

hook: On older cloud disks, a small but busy database had to buy space it would never fill. Why?
title: Clouds sell disk speed three ways. Know which you bought.
body:
On older volume types, such as AWS gp2 and Azure Premium SSD, IOPS grow with capacity. A small, busy database must buy a big disk just to get IOPS. That is **performance tied to size**.

Newer types, such as AWS gp3 and io2, Azure Premium SSD v2 and Ultra, and Google Hyperdisk, use **provisioned performance**: capacity, IOPS and throughput are set separately. The third model is **burst credits**: small volumes run above baseline for a while, spending from a credit bucket.
takeaway: Buy space for your data and speed for your workload, separately.
deeper:
**Why the shift:** Size-tied pricing makes capacity a proxy for speed. A database that is small but I/O-hungry pays for storage it never fills. Provisioned models decouple the dimensions, so you pay for what the workload consumes.

**Azure shows the spread:** Premium SSD ties performance to its size tier. Premium SSD v2 includes a free baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s, and lets you raise each dimension separately. Ultra Disk lets you change performance at runtime.

**The catch with bursts:** Credits suit spiky, mostly idle volumes. But a volume that benchmarks well during a burst drops to its much lower baseline once the bucket drains, often in the middle of sustained load. The benchmark measured the savings account, not the salary.

**What to check:** Which model the type uses, its sustained baseline, and whether space or performance is driving your purchase.

quiz.q: A load test on a small burst-credit volume looks great for 20 minutes, then latency jumps under the same load. What happened?
quiz.a: The credit bucket drained. The volume was running above its baseline on credits and has fallen back to its much lower sustained performance.

mcq.q: Which of these volume types ties IOPS to capacity?
options: AWS gp2
AWS gp3
Azure Premium SSD v2
Google Hyperdisk
mcq.why: gp2, like Azure Premium SSD, gives IOPS in proportion to size. gp3, Premium SSD v2 and Hyperdisk provision performance separately.

hook: Daily snapshots of a 1 TiB volume don't add 1 TiB a day to your storage.
title: Snapshots store only what changed
body:
A **snapshot** is a point-in-time copy of a volume, and cloud snapshots are incremental. The first one stores every block that has been written. Each later snapshot stores only the blocks that changed since the previous one.

So a mostly static volume adds little per snapshot, and frequent backups stay cheap. There's a durability bonus too: AWS stores EBS snapshots in S3-backed storage, far more durable than the volume itself.
takeaway: The first snapshot copies the disk. Every one after copies the diff.
deeper:
**The economics:** On a 1 TiB volume where a few GiB change per day, each daily snapshot after the first costs only those few GiB. That makes frequent snapshots practical.

**The durability gap:** An EBS volume is replicated inside one Availability Zone and rated around 99.8-99.9% annual durability. Its snapshots live in S3-backed storage, and S3 is built for 11 nines. The snapshot is your backstop when the volume, or its zone, is gone.

**Beyond backup:** In Kubernetes, a new PersistentVolumeClaim can be created from a snapshot, or cloned from another claim, to spin up test copies or recover from mistakes.

**The catch:** A snapshot captures blocks, not application state. By default it looks like a disk after a sudden power cut, not a cleanly shut-down database.

quiz.q: A 2 TiB volume has about 1% of its blocks change per day. Roughly how much does the tenth daily snapshot add?
quiz.a: About 20 GiB: only the blocks changed since the ninth snapshot. Only the first snapshot stores every written block.

mcq.q: What does the second snapshot of a cloud volume store?
options: Only blocks changed since the first
Every block on the volume again
Only the filesystem metadata
A compressed copy of the whole volume
mcq.why: Cloud snapshots are incremental: the first stores all written blocks, later ones only the blocks that changed.

hook: You restore a database from a snapshot, and the first thing it does is run crash recovery.
title: A snapshot is a disk after someone pulled the plug
body:
A cloud snapshot is **crash-consistent**: it looks exactly like the disk after a power cut. Blocks already on the volume are captured. Writes still sitting in the OS page cache, never flushed, are missing.

That's why a database restored from one recovers the same way it does after a crash, by replaying its **write-ahead log**. For an **application-consistent** snapshot, freeze the filesystem or tell the database to checkpoint first.
takeaway: Storage sees blocks, not transactions. Coordinate first, or plan to recover.
deeper:
**Why it happens:** The storage system only sees blocks. It can't know which ones form a complete transaction or which writes are still in the VM's memory. A snapshot at an arbitrary moment freezes whatever half-finished state the volume is in. The power-cut comparison is exact: in both cases, flushed blocks survive and unflushed page-cache data is gone.

**Why databases cope:** Well-built databases are designed for exactly this. On startup they read the WAL and replay or roll back work until the data files are consistent. Anything written with plain `write()` but never `fsync`'d simply never reached the volume.

**When that's not enough:**
1. Freeze the filesystem, or ask the database to checkpoint.
2. Take the snapshot.
3. Resume writes.

Kubernetes VolumeSnapshots follow the same rule: crash-consistent by default.

quiz.q: An app saves a record with write() and reports success. A snapshot is taken, and the restored copy lacks the record. Is the snapshot broken?
quiz.a: No. write() only reached the page cache. The snapshot captures blocks on the volume, like a power cut, so unflushed data is missing. Only fsync makes it durable.

mcq.q: How do you get an application-consistent snapshot?
options: Freeze the filesystem or checkpoint first
Take two snapshots and compare them
Store the snapshot in S3-backed storage
Use an incremental snapshot type
mcq.why: Freezing or checkpointing makes the on-disk state complete before the block copy, instead of relying on crash recovery afterwards.

hook: EBS started on hard drives doing 120-150 IOPS each. How far has it come since 2008?
title: EBS went from 150-IOPS drives to 140 trillion ops a day
body:
AWS launched EBS on August 20, 2008, as network block storage for EC2. It ran on hard drives: about 120-150 IOPS per drive, 6-8 ms average latency. The first SSD-backed type arrived in August 2012, capped at 1,000 IOPS.

By 2024, Marc Olson wrote that EBS delivers over 140 trillion operations daily across an SSD fleet. It can give a single instance more IOPS than an entire Availability Zone could get in the early years.

stat.label: EBS operations per day, per AWS in 2024

takeaway: Keep the interface boring and you can rebuild everything underneath it.
deeper:
**Same interface, new machine:** Customers always saw a block device attached to their instance. Underneath, almost everything changed.
1. Media moved from hard drives to SSD, starting in 2012.
2. From 2013-2014, storage processing moved off the host CPU onto dedicated Nitro cards.
3. AWS built its own transport, SRD, whose foundation was laid in 2014.

**Calibrate the gap:** The original design averaged 6-8 ms per I/O. io2 Block Express is designed for average latency under 500 microseconds for 16 KiB I/O. That is more than ten times faster, and by Little's Law it means more IOPS per unit of concurrency and higher commit rates.

**The real hard part:** Raw media speed wasn't the long fight. Much of EBS's later engineering went into isolation from noisy neighbors and a control plane that could survive its own failures.

quiz.q: EBS kept the same block-device interface from 2008 to 2024 while swapping media, offload hardware and network transport. Why was a fixed interface valuable?
quiz.a: Customers' databases and filesystems kept working unchanged while AWS replaced hard drives with SSDs, moved processing to Nitro and built SRD, gaining orders of magnitude in performance.

mcq.q: What did the first EBS volumes run on in 2008?
options: Hard drives at about 120-150 IOPS each
SSDs capped at 1,000 IOPS each
Local NVMe behind Nitro cards
SSDs connected over SRD transport
mcq.why: EBS launched on hard drives with 6-8 ms average latency. The first SSD-backed type came in August 2012.

hook: In early EBS, your database could slow down because of a customer you'd never met.
title: Noisy neighbors: one busy tenant slows everyone
body:
Early EBS packed many customers' volumes onto the same physical disks and the same network. Sharing is what makes cloud storage cheap. It also meant one busy customer could slow everyone else on that hardware: the **noisy neighbor** problem.

For databases that need predictable latency, this was a serious flaw. AWS attacked it over many years on three fronts: better queueing and isolation, the move from hard drives to SSD, and moving the storage client off the host CPU.
takeaway: Sharing makes storage cheap. Isolation is what makes sharing tolerable.
deeper:
**Why hard drives made it worse:** At about 120-150 IOPS per drive, a single aggressive workload could saturate a spindle, and every other tenant on it waited. SSDs deliver vastly more IOPS per device, so the same contention does far less damage.

**Three fixes, three causes:**
1. Queueing and isolation share capacity fairly among tenants.
2. SSDs make each device much harder to saturate.
3. Nitro cards took storage processing out of the hypervisor on the host CPU, where it added jitter and stole cycles from customers.

**It never fully goes away:** In Kubernetes, pods on the same node share network bandwidth to EBS and the instance's EBS limits. A heavy database pod can starve its neighbors. The standard fix is to put heavy databases on dedicated node pools.

quiz.q: Two database pods share a node, each with its own EBS volume. One starts a huge scan and the other's latency spikes. Why, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: Both pods share the node's network bandwidth to EBS and the instance's EBS limits. Put heavy databases on dedicated node pools.

mcq.q: Why did moving from hard drives to SSDs ease EBS's noisy-neighbor problem?
options: Each device had far more IOPS to share
SSDs gave every tenant a private disk
SSDs removed the network hop entirely
SSDs made replication unnecessary
mcq.why: At 120-150 IOPS per drive, one tenant could saturate a spindle. SSDs offer far more IOPS, so contention hurts neighbors less.

hook: EBS writes need no voting. So why does EBS need a strongly consistent database at all?
title: Chain replication is easy. Changing the chain is hard.
body:
An EBS volume is replicated inside one Availability Zone. In the simplified model from AWS's Physalia paper, it uses **chain replication**: writes flow from the EC2 host to a primary storage server, then to a replica, before being acknowledged. No coordination needed.

Failure changes that. A new replica must be chosen, data re-mirrored, and everyone must agree which copy is primary. That agreement needs a strongly consistent **configuration master**.
takeaway: The data path can stay simple only if the control path is strict.
deeper:
**Why the happy path is fast:** No voting happens on each write. It's a pipeline, host to primary to replica, then acknowledge, which keeps latency low.

**Where the complexity hides:** When the primary or replica fails, the system must:
1. Pick a replacement server.
2. Copy the data to it (re-mirroring).
3. Make sure every party agrees on exactly one primary.

**Why step 3 is non-negotiable:** If two servers each believed they were primary, clients could write divergent data. For a block device, that's catastrophic. So who is in the chain, and who leads, must live in a store everyone trusts.

**The catch:** That configuration master holds little data but is critical for availability. If it can't answer, any volume that needs to reconfigure is stuck. The 2011 EBS outage showed what happens when it is shared and overloaded. Note the scope too: an EBS volume does not survive the loss of its AZ.

quiz.q: After an EBS server failure, two surviving servers each briefly believe they are primary. Why is this the outcome the design must prevent?
quiz.a: Clients could send writes to both and the copies would diverge, corrupting the volume. That's why chain membership and the primary live in a strongly consistent configuration master.

mcq.q: In EBS chain replication, when is coordination required?
options: When a server fails and the chain changes
On every write, before acknowledging
Only when a snapshot is taken
Whenever a volume attaches to a VM
mcq.why: Normal writes just flow host to primary to replica. Reconfiguration after a failure needs agreement on the new chain and primary.

hook: In 2011, a bad network change in one AWS zone slowed API calls in the other zones too.
title: 2011: one zone's network fault became a regional problem
body:
On April 21, 2011, an incorrect network change isolated many EBS nodes in one Availability Zone at once. When connectivity returned, they all tried to re-mirror at the same time. This **re-mirroring storm** ran out of free capacity, and volumes got stuck.

The replication configuration lived in the EBS control plane, in a database shared with API traffic. The storm of negotiations overloaded it, and API calls for other AZs in the region degraded too.

stat.label: of EBS volumes in the AZ stuck, April 2011

takeaway: Every node doing the right thing at once can be the wrong thing.
deeper:
**The cascade, step by step:**
1. A network change isolates many EBS nodes in one AZ.
2. Connectivity returns, and every node re-mirrors at once.
3. Free capacity runs out, so volumes can't finish and stay stuck.
4. Each attempt negotiates configuration in a shared control-plane database.
5. Its thread pools fill, and API calls for other AZs degrade.

**Correct locally, wrong globally:** Each node's reaction, re-mirror when you lose your partner, was right in isolation. Done by many nodes simultaneously, it exhausted the spare capacity that re-mirroring needs.

**The real lesson:** A fault in one zone's network became a regional control-plane problem only because of a shared dependency. AWS's lesson was about blast radius, and its answer was Physalia, which splits configuration into millions of independent cells.

quiz.q: Your system re-copies data the instant a node loses its replica partner. A network fault cuts hundreds of nodes off from their partners at once. What can go wrong?
quiz.a: A re-mirroring storm, as in EBS 2011: every node copies at once, spare capacity runs out, volumes get stuck, and any shared coordination database gets overloaded, spreading the damage.

mcq.q: In the 2011 EBS outage, why did other AZs in the region degrade?
options: Configuration lived in a database shared with API traffic
Their volumes were chain-replicated into the failed AZ
The bad network change was applied to every AZ
Their snapshots were stored inside the failed AZ
mcq.why: The re-mirroring storm overloaded the shared control-plane database. Its thread pools filled, degrading API calls region-wide.

hook: Your configuration database has never failed. Why might it still be the riskiest thing you run?
title: A shared dependency's blast radius is everyone
body:
**Blast radius** is the set of customers hurt by a single failure. EBS learned it the hard way in 2011: one configuration database served the whole region, so a problem in one zone hurt everyone who depended on it.

Reliability on paper doesn't shrink blast radius. Rare failures still happen, and overload can arrive from somewhere unexpected, like a recovery storm. What shrinks it is splitting shared dependencies, so any one failure touches only a small slice of customers.
takeaway: Don't ask how often it fails. Ask who breaks when it does.
deeper:
**Turn goals into a question:** If this component fails or gets overloaded, who notices? A single global database, configuration service or shared queue has a blast radius equal to everyone using it.

**How to shrink it:** Partition. Run many independent copies of a service, each serving a subset of customers and not coordinating with the others, so a failure in one cannot cascade.

**The cost:** More units to deploy, monitor and manage. You trade operational simplicity for containment.

**The extreme version:** In 2011, EBS configuration lived in one control-plane database shared with regional API traffic. The redesign, Physalia, partitions all the way down: each cell holds the configuration for roughly one volume.

**Where to look first:** Configuration stores. They're small, easy to overlook and critical to everything, which is exactly the profile of a dependency with an enormous blast radius.

quiz.q: Design A: one config database with 99.99% uptime serving all customers. Design B: 1,000 independent cells at 99.9% each. Which has the smaller blast radius?
quiz.a: Design B. A cell failure hurts only that cell's customers. Any failure of the single database, however rare, hurts everyone at once.

mcq.q: What does "blast radius" measure?
options: The customers hurt by a single failure
How often a component fails per year
How far data is replicated geographically
How long recovery takes after a failure
mcq.why: Blast radius is the set of customers affected when one thing breaks. Shrinking it means partitioning shared dependencies.

hook: After 2011, AWS rebuilt the store that decides which EBS server is primary. It isn't one database.

predict.q: How many independent Paxos groups does Physalia run to hold EBS volume configuration?
options: Millions, roughly one per volume
One per region
One per Availability Zone

title: Physalia: millions of tiny Paxos databases, one per volume
body:
**Physalia** (NSDI 2020) is AWS's transactional key-value store built to be the configuration master for EBS. Instead of one big database, it runs a colony of many small **cells**.

Each cell stores the configuration for a single partition key, roughly one volume. It runs **Paxos** among a small set of nodes, seven in the paper's description, and never coordinates with any other cell. One physical node can host many cells. A problem in one cell touches only the volumes it configures.
takeaway: Shrink the unit of failure until it's one customer's problem.
deeper:
**Aimed at 2011:** Back then, one shared configuration database was overwhelmed by a re-mirroring storm. With Physalia, each volume's configuration lives in its own small consensus group. An overloaded cell hurts its own volumes and nobody else's.

**Consistency where it's needed:** Paxos inside each cell gives chain replication what it requires: one agreed answer to which server is primary. No cross-cell coordination means cells can't drag each other down.

**Why seven:** A majority of seven survives up to three simultaneous node failures, and the nodes are spread across racks and power domains.

**Why it's affordable:** Packing many cells onto each node keeps the hardware footprint reasonable, even with millions of cells.

**The pattern:** This is cell-based architecture for a control plane, taken to the limit. The unit of isolation is roughly one customer resource, so any single failure's blast radius is tiny.

quiz.q: Why not run one large, well-provisioned Paxos cluster for all EBS configuration instead of millions of small ones?
quiz.a: Its blast radius would be every volume. Any overload, like a re-mirroring storm, would hurt everyone. Independent cells confine a failure to the volumes in the affected cells.

mcq.q: What does each Physalia cell store?
options: Configuration for roughly one volume
The data blocks of one volume
Configuration for one whole AZ
Snapshots for one customer account
mcq.why: Each cell holds configuration for a single partition key, roughly one volume, and runs Paxos independently of all other cells.

hook: How can a database stay strongly consistent and highly available when CAP says you can't have both?
title: Physalia gives up "everywhere" to keep consistency
body:
The **CAP theorem** says a system can't be both available and consistent everywhere during a network partition. Physalia doesn't try to beat that.

It narrows the goal instead: be extremely available for the keys each client needs, for the clients that need them. A volume's configuration only matters to the EC2 instance using the volume and the storage servers holding it. If some unrelated machine can't reach that cell, nothing is lost. So Physalia keeps strong consistency and aims availability only where it counts.
takeaway: Define availability per key and per client, and consistency gets cheap.
deeper:
**The usual framing:** Can any client reach any data? Under a partition, CAP forces a choice between answering with possibly inconsistent data and refusing to answer.

**The narrower question:** Can the clients who need this key reach it? For EBS configuration, that's a tiny set: one instance and a few storage servers. A partition that hides the cell from everyone else costs nothing.

**How it becomes real:** The goal only works because of placement. Physalia puts each cell's nodes near its clients, so a partition separating the cell from them would usually separate the instance from its data too.

**The catch:** This works because EBS configuration has a small, known set of interested parties. A key that many scattered clients all need can't sit near all of them.

**The lesson:** For any control plane, ask who actually needs each key before deciding strong consistency is too expensive.

quiz.q: During a partition, a Physalia cell is unreachable from half the region but reachable from its volume's instance and storage servers. Is that an outage?
quiz.a: No. Only that instance and those servers need the volume's configuration. Physalia targets availability for the clients that need each key, not global reachability.

mcq.q: How does Physalia deal with the CAP theorem?
options: It targets availability only for clients each key needs
It relaxes to eventual consistency during partitions
It avoids partitions with a dedicated network
It keeps a global copy readable from any client
mcq.why: Physalia keeps strong consistency and aims for extreme availability only for the keys each client needs, for the clients that need them.

hook: Physalia deliberately puts each volume's control plane where it will fail at the same moment as the data.

predict.q: Where should Physalia place the cell holding one volume's configuration?
options: Near the volume's instance and storage servers
In a central, heavily protected location
Spread evenly across every AZ in the region

title: Put the control plane where it fails with the data
body:
Physalia places each cell's nodes close, in network topology, to the only parties that care about that volume's configuration: the EC2 instance using it and the storage servers holding it.

That makes the control plane **share fate** with the data path. A partition that cuts the cell off from its volume almost certainly cuts the instance off from its data too. The volume is unusable anyway, so the unreachable cell adds little extra unavailability. As clients move, their cells move with them.
takeaway: A control plane that fails with its data plane never fails alone.
deeper:
**The alternative, and its flaw:** Store configuration in a distant central location. Now a partition between the instance's rack and that location blocks reconfiguration, even though the instance and its storage servers can still talk perfectly well. The outage comes purely from the control plane.

**Overlapping failure domains:** Co-locating the cell with the data path means the two tend to fail together. The control plane rarely causes an outage on its own.

**Cells follow clients:** Instances move and volumes get re-mirrored to new servers, so cells migrate too, staying near wherever their clients are.

**The balance:** Close is not the same as clustered. A cell's seven nodes are spread over enough racks and power domains that small failures don't stop it. Near enough to share fate with its clients, spread enough that one rack or power fault can't take out a majority.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes moving all Physalia cells into one hardened central cluster to simplify operations. What availability problem does that create?
quiz.a: A partition between a volume's instance and the central cluster would block reconfiguration while the instance and storage servers can still talk, adding outages caused only by the control plane.

mcq.q: Why is it acceptable for a Physalia cell to be unreachable during a partition that also isolates its volume?
options: The instance has lost its data path anyway
Another cell takes over the volume instantly
The instance caches configuration forever
EBS writes never read the configuration
mcq.why: The cell sits near the instance and storage servers, so a partition isolating it likely isolates the data too; little extra unavailability results.

hook: Physalia runs millions of Paxos cells. A bug too rare to find in testing will still fire. How do you catch it?
title: Physalia's cells are spread out and model-checked
body:
A cell placed close to its volume has a hidden risk. If all seven nodes share one rack, a single power event removes a majority and Paxos stops. So Physalia spreads each cell's nodes over enough racks and power domains that small failures do not halt it.

The second risk is bugs. The team specified the protocol in **TLA+**, ran a model checker over it, and tested the real code with **Jepsen**.
takeaway: At a million copies, rare bugs are daily bugs. Check the protocol formally.
deeper:
**Placement versus diversity:** Physalia puts each cell near the instance and storage servers it serves. Taken too far, that packs a cell into one failure domain. Spreading nodes across racks and power domains inside that neighbourhood keeps a majority alive through the small failures a large fleet sees constantly.

**Why tests are not enough:** a consensus protocol running in millions of cells will eventually hit every rare ordering of messages, crashes and restarts. A bug too rare to see in testing becomes routine at that scale.

**Two tools, two layers:** TLA+ gives a precise specification, and a model checker explores its states looking for violations such as two primaries for one volume. Jepsen attacks the running implementation with injected faults like network partitions.

**The catch:** a model check covers the spec, not the code, which is why the team did both. For a system that decides which copy of a customer's disk is authoritative, a subtle bug means corrupted data, not a slow request.

quiz.q: Your team's new consensus protocol passed months of fault-injection tests. It will run in a million independent groups. Why might that not be enough?
quiz.a: Across a million groups, rare interleavings of messages and crashes will happen that tests never hit. Model checking a formal spec, as Physalia did with TLA+, explores those states systematically.

mcq.q: Why does Physalia spread one cell's nodes across racks and power domains?
options: So one rack or power failure cannot remove a Paxos majority
So cells can coordinate with neighbouring cells during failures
So the cell sits closer to the volume's EC2 instance
So the model checker can treat every node as independent
mcq.why: Seven nodes in one rack share its fate. Spreading them keeps a majority alive, so the cell keeps reaching consensus through small failures.

hook: Your config store holds a few megabytes and sees little traffic. Why is it the scariest box on the diagram?
title: The smallest dependency can have the biggest blast radius
body:
Configuration stores look harmless: little data, light traffic, simple schema. So teams put them in one shared database. But they are hit hardest during failures, exactly when everything reconfigures at once. In 2011 that pattern overloaded the EBS control plane and degraded API calls across a region.

Physalia is the clearest published fix: a **cell-based architecture** where many small, independent cells each serve a few customers. A global database gives a global **blast radius**. Tiny cells give a tiny one.
takeaway: A system is only as isolated as its most shared dependency.
deeper:
**The review question:** for every shared dependency, ask "If this breaks, how many customers break with it?" An answer of "all of them" is the finding.

**Why failures feed it:** steady-state load says nothing about recovery load. In the 2011 EBS outage, a storm of re-mirroring negotiations filled the control plane's thread pools, and API calls for other AZs in the region degraded too.

**An analogy that maps:** a ship's watertight compartments. Each compartment is a cell, and a breach floods one, not the hull. The mapping holds only if compartments share nothing, which is why Physalia cells do not coordinate with each other.

**How far to go:** Physalia goes to roughly one cell per volume and places each cell near its clients. You rarely need that granularity. But estimate the fraction of customers each component can take down, name what could overload it during recovery, and ask whether it can be split.

quiz.q: A new service stores feature flags for every tenant in one small, lightly loaded database. During a regional incident, every service restarts at once. What risk does this design carry?
quiz.a: A global blast radius. Mass restarts hit the flag store together, and if it overloads, every tenant fails. Splitting it into independent cells confines an overload to a few tenants.

mcq.q: What made the pre-Physalia EBS configuration store a region-wide risk?
options: It shared one control-plane database with API traffic
It stored configuration on the same disks as volumes
It ran a single Paxos group across every zone
It was placed too close to the EC2 instances
mcq.why: Replication config lived in a control-plane database shared with API traffic, so a re-mirroring storm in one AZ degraded API calls across the region.

hook: Early EBS stole CPU from the very customers it served. Where did AWS move the work?
title: Nitro moved EBS off the host CPU and onto a card
body: Early EBS clients ran in the hypervisor on the host CPU. That added **jitter**, unpredictable latency, and stole cycles from customers. Starting in 2013-2014, AWS moved storage processing onto dedicated **Nitro cards**. On Nitro instances, an EBS volume appears to the guest as an ordinary NVMe device. The card handles the network protocol, encryption and I/O processing, so that work no longer runs in the hypervisor on the host CPU.
takeaway: Move the noisy work onto its own hardware, and the noise goes with it.
deeper:
**Two problems, one move:** storage processing in the hypervisor shared host cores with guest workloads, so busy moments showed up as jitter in your I/O and as cycles taken from your app. Moving it to a dedicated card takes it off those shared cores.

**The disguise:** the guest OS sees and drives an ordinary NVMe device with its standard driver. The blocks actually live on storage servers across the network. That is why EBS itself counts as disaggregated storage: Nitro presents a remote volume as local NVMe.

**What else rides on the card:** the network protocol and encryption. For io2 Block Express, AWS says the instance talks to storage using SRD, implemented on the Nitro card dedicated to EBS.

**The long game:** Nitro was one front in a years-long fight against noisy neighbours, alongside better queueing and isolation and the move to SSD. Together with SRD, it helped bring io2 Block Express under 0.5 ms average latency.

quiz.q: Two VMs run identical databases on identical EBS volumes. One is on an old hypervisor-based host, one on Nitro. Why might the Nitro VM show steadier I/O latency?
quiz.a: On the old host, the EBS client ran in the hypervisor on the host CPU, adding jitter. Nitro does storage processing on a dedicated card, removing that source of variance.

mcq.q: On a Nitro instance, how does an EBS volume appear to the guest operating system?
options: As an ordinary NVMe device
As a paravirtual network share
As an iSCSI target over TCP
As a local SATA hard drive
mcq.why: The Nitro card presents the remote volume as NVMe and handles the network protocol, encryption and I/O, so the guest drives it like any NVMe disk.

hook: Some of your slowest storage I/Os aren't waiting on a disk at all. They're stuck on one busy network path.
title: SRD sprays one flow across many paths to cut the tail
body:
On a busy datacenter network, any single path can congest. A flow pinned to that path waits, even while other paths sit idle, and those stuck I/Os become your slow tail.

AWS built **SRD** (Scalable Reliable Datagram), a transport whose foundation was laid in 2014. It sprays the packets of one flow across many network paths and handles reordering and retransmission in hardware. For io2 Block Express, AWS says the instance talks to storage using SRD on the Nitro card dedicated to EBS.
takeaway: Don't queue in the slowest lane. Use every lane and sort it out after.
deeper:
**Why the tail matters:** a database transaction, or a request touching many blocks, waits for its slowest I/O. The median can look great while users feel the p99.

**How spraying helps:** traditional transports usually keep a flow on one path so packets arrive in order. SRD spreads each flow across many paths, so congestion on one path delays only a fraction of the packets instead of all of them.

**The price of spraying:** packets now arrive out of order, and some are lost on bad paths. SRD handles reordering and retransmission in hardware on the Nitro card, so the fix does not burn host CPU.

**Where it lands:** io2 Block Express, which AWS designs for average latency under 500 microseconds for 16 KiB I/O. Nitro and SRD together moved EBS processing off the host and cut that latency.

quiz.q: Your storage client pins each flow to one network path. Average latency is fine, but p99 is terrible under load. What would SRD-style spraying change?
quiz.a: Congestion on one path would delay only a fraction of each flow's packets, not the whole flow, so the rare very slow I/Os become rarer. Hardware handles the reordering and retransmits.

mcq.q: What does SRD do with the packets of a single flow?
options: Sprays them across many network paths
Pins them to the least-loaded single path
Batches them into larger jumbo frames
Duplicates them on two paths, keeps the first
mcq.why: SRD spreads one flow's packets over many paths and reorders and retransmits in hardware, so one congested path cannot stall the whole flow.

hook: Six EBS volume types share one durability rating, except one. Which one breaks ranks?

predict.q: Which EBS volume type does AWS state at 99.999% annual durability?
options: io2 Block Express
gp3
st1

title: Only one EBS volume type is stated at 99.999% durable
body:
gp3 and io2 Block Express sound like siblings. The table says otherwise. As of 2026, gp3 reaches 80,000 IOPS, 2,000 MiB/s and 64 TiB, while gp2, io1, st1 and sc1 all cap at 16 TiB. **io2 Block Express** tops the table: 256,000 IOPS, 4,000 MiB/s and 64 TiB, designed for under 500 µs average latency on 16 KiB I/O.

It is also the only type stated at 99.999% durability. Every other type, gp3 included, is stated at 99.8-99.9%.
takeaway: Read the durability column before the IOPS column.
deeper:
**The workhorse:** gp3 is the provisioned successor to gp2. It lifts the ceiling from 16,000 IOPS and 250 MiB/s to 80,000 and 2,000, and lets you set IOPS and throughput apart from size.

**The high end:** io2 Block Express became generally available in July 2021, and AWS described it as "the first SAN built for the cloud". It adds latency and durability, not just IOPS.

**The HDD tiers:** st1 and sc1 quote 500 and 250 IOPS at 1 MiB I/O, with 500 and 250 MiB/s. Spinning disks only do well on large sequential transfers, so these suit log scans and bulk data, never random database I/O.

**How to choose:**
1. Find the I/O size and pattern.
2. Check whether sustained IOPS and throughput fit gp3.
3. Ask whether latency or durability justifies io2 Block Express.
4. Plan snapshots and replicas either way.

quiz.q: A team moves a random-read database from gp3 to st1 because st1 is cheaper and its 500 MiB/s covers their bandwidth. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: st1 is a hard-drive type rated at 500 IOPS with 1 MiB I/Os. Small random reads get only a sliver of that throughput, so the database slows dramatically.

mcq.q: Which EBS volume type has the highest IOPS limit in AWS's 2026 table?
options: io2 Block Express, at 256,000 IOPS
gp3, at 80,000 IOPS
io1, at 64,000 IOPS
gp2, at 16,000 IOPS
mcq.why: io2 Block Express tops out at 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s, more than three times gp3's 80,000 IOPS.

hook: You run 5,000 EBS volumes, each rated 99.9% durable. How many will you lose this year?
title: At 99.9% durable, a big fleet loses volumes every year

stat.label: volume losses a year in a 5,000-volume fleet

body:
99.9% sounds safe until you read it as an annual loss rate. EBS gp3 is stated at 99.8-99.9% durability, so 1 to 2 volumes in 1,000 are lost per year. A 5,000-volume fleet should expect roughly 5 to 10 losses, while S3 is stated at 11 nines.

At fleet scale, a lost volume is not a freak event. It is a yearly line item you plan for with snapshots, replicas or both.
takeaway: Durable enough to hold your data is not durable enough to be its only copy.
deeper:
**Reading the percentage:** durability is a yearly failure rate across a fleet. 99.8-99.9% means 0.1-0.2% of volumes lost per year. At 1,000 volumes that is one or two. At 5,000, five to ten.

**The one exception:** io2 Block Express is stated at 99.999%. Far better, and still well below object storage.

**What actually protects you:**
1. Snapshots, stored in S3-backed storage, give a recoverable copy outside the volume.
2. Replicas in other Availability Zones cover volume loss and the loss of a whole AZ, which EBS alone does not survive because it replicates inside one zone.

**The catch:** a snapshot is crash-consistent and only as fresh as the last one you took. For data that cannot lose recent writes, you need a live replica, not just snapshots.

quiz.q: Your startup's only database copy lives on one gp3 volume, and it has never failed in three years. Your CTO says that proves EBS is safe enough. What's wrong with that reasoning?
quiz.a: At 0.1-0.2% annual loss, one volume usually survives for years, but the risk is real and grows with fleet size. With no snapshot or replica, a single loss is total data loss.

mcq.q: What does 99.8-99.9% annual durability mean for an EBS fleet?
options: About 1 to 2 volumes in 1,000 lost per year
About 1 to 2 volumes in a million lost per year
About 1 to 2 blocks per volume lost per year
About 1 to 2 hours of downtime per year
mcq.why: Durability is an annual loss rate: 0.1-0.2% of volumes, so 1-2 per 1,000 each year. Downtime measures availability, a different thing.

hook: Replicated, managed, and run by AWS. Your EBS volume still can't survive one kind of failure.
title: EBS is replicated, but only inside one zone
body:
Replicated and managed sounds like S3. It is not. EBS replicates each volume inside one **Availability Zone**, so every copy shares that zone's fate. It does not survive an AZ loss. Its annual failure rate is measured in tenths of a percent, not S3's 11 nines.

The fix is architectural. Run database replicas in other AZs, and take snapshots, which are kept in S3-backed storage.
takeaway: Replicated inside one zone still means one zone away from zero.
deeper:
**Two separate gaps:** scope and rate. Scope: replication inside one AZ covers a failed server or disk, not a failed zone. Only copies outside the zone help there. Rate: even with every zone healthy, 0.1-0.2% of volumes are lost each year.

**Two separate fixes:** replicas in other AZs close the scope gap. Snapshots close the rate gap by keeping a recoverable copy in S3-backed storage.

**Why AWS is different:** Azure offers ZRS disks replicated synchronously across three zones, and Google offers Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability across two zones. AWS keeps EBS volumes single-AZ and pushes cross-AZ durability to the application or to managed databases.

**The design rule:** on AWS, cross-zone durability is your job, not the disk's. Draw your database topology assuming any single volume, or any single zone, can vanish.

quiz.q: An architect says: 'We don't need cross-AZ replicas. EBS already keeps multiple copies of every volume.' What two risks does this ignore?
quiz.a: An AZ failure takes every EBS copy at once, since replication is only inside one zone. And 0.1-0.2% of volumes are lost yearly anyway. Cross-AZ replicas and snapshots cover both.

mcq.q: Why doesn't an EBS volume survive the loss of its Availability Zone?
options: All its replicas live inside that one zone
Its snapshots are stored inside that zone
It is replicated to only a single disk
Its chain replication waits on a second zone
mcq.why: EBS replicates within one AZ. A zone failure takes every copy together, so only replicas or snapshots outside the zone help.

section: 4.3 Google Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk and Azure Managed Disks
hook: AWS built EBS as its own system. Google's VM disks sit on something much bigger. What?
title: Google's VM disks sit on the same storage as YouTube
body: There are two ways to build cloud block storage. AWS chose a dedicated system: EBS is separate, with its own replication and control plane. Google chose to layer. **Persistent Disk**, network block storage for Compute Engine, runs on **Colossus**, Google's cluster filesystem. Google lists Compute Engine VMs among Colossus's clients, so its block storage shares one substrate with Cloud Storage and YouTube. Either way, the VM sees a network disk whose life is separate from the machine.
takeaway: A block volume can be its own system, or a view over a bigger one.
deeper:
**The AWS route:** EBS is its own stack. It has chain replication inside one AZ, Physalia as its configuration master, and SRD as its transport on Nitro cards.

**The Google route:** block storage becomes one more client of a shared platform. The same substrate serves Cloud Storage and YouTube, so every Persistent Disk rests on that platform's scale.

**A third example:** Alibaba's Pangu follows the layered pattern too. It is a unified storage platform underneath Alibaba Cloud's Elastic Block Storage, object storage, NAS and PolarDB.

**What users actually see:** mostly the same product. The visible change on Google's side is the newer Hyperdisk generation, which provisions capacity, IOPS and throughput separately and comes in variants for different jobs, much like AWS gp3 and Azure Premium SSD v2.

quiz.q: A colleague says Google Persistent Disk and AWS EBS must share an architecture, because both appear to the VM as network disks. What's the key difference?
quiz.a: EBS is a separate, dedicated block storage system. Persistent Disk sits on Colossus, Google's shared cluster filesystem, which also serves Cloud Storage and YouTube.

mcq.q: What does Google Persistent Disk share its underlying storage substrate with?
options: Cloud Storage and YouTube, via Colossus
Nothing: it is a dedicated block system
Only other Compute Engine VM disks
AWS EBS, through a shared interconnect
mcq.why: Google lists Compute Engine VMs among the clients of Colossus, the cluster filesystem that also serves Cloud Storage and YouTube.

section: 4.3 Google Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk and Azure Managed Disks
hook: One disk type can't be the best at IOPS, scans and surviving a zone loss. So Google stopped trying.
title: Hyperdisk splits one disk into a variant per job
body: One disk type cannot be the best at random IOPS, sequential scans and zone survival at once. **Hyperdisk**, Google's newer generation, provisions capacity, IOPS and throughput separately and splits into variants. Balanced is general purpose: up to 160,000 IOPS and 2,400 MiB/s, attachable read-write to up to 8 instances. Balanced High Availability replicates synchronously across two zones. Extreme reaches 350,000 IOPS for large databases. Throughput targets analytics scans.
takeaway: Buy the dimension your workload saturates, not the whole bundle.
deeper:
**Balanced, multi-writer:** read-write attach to up to 8 instances is unusual for block storage. A block device has no locking, so multiple writers need software that coordinates access, such as a cluster-aware filesystem or database.

**Balanced High Availability:** synchronous replication across two zones in a region means a single-zone failure does not lose the volume. AWS EBS, by contrast, stays single-AZ.

**Extreme:** a ceiling of 350,000 IOPS, above io2 Block Express's 256,000 on AWS.

**Throughput:** tuned for sequential analytics scans, where bytes per second matter more than operations per second.

**The pattern:** throughput = IOPS × I/O size, and workloads hit different caps. Instead of one type that is mediocre everywhere, providers offer independent knobs and tuned variants, so each workload buys the cap it actually hits.

quiz.q: Two teams share a Hyperdisk Balanced volume attached read-write to three VMs, each mounting ext4 directly. Why is this dangerous?
quiz.a: A block device has no locking, and ext4 assumes it is the only writer. Three independent mounts will overwrite each other's metadata and corrupt the filesystem. Multi-writer attach needs coordinating software.

mcq.q: Which Hyperdisk variant keeps a volume alive through a single-zone failure?
options: Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability
Hyperdisk Extreme
Hyperdisk Throughput
Hyperdisk ML
mcq.why: Balanced High Availability replicates synchronously across two zones in a region, so losing one zone does not lose the volume.

section: 4.3 Google Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk and Azure Managed Disks
hook: A training fleet of 2,500 machines needs the same model weights. What if they all mounted one disk?
title: Hyperdisk ML: 2,500 nodes reading at 1.2 TB/s
body:
ML fleets need the same large files, model weights and training data, on every node. Copying them to each machine separately is slow and wasteful. **Hyperdisk ML** attaches one volume read-only to up to 2,500 instances. Because nobody writes, there are no writers to coordinate, so the fan-out is safe. Google reported 2,500 nodes reading at 1.2 TB/s.

Hyperdisk also offers **storage pools**: buy capacity and performance in bulk and share them across many disks.
takeaway: Take away the writers, and one disk can have thousands of readers.
deeper:
**Why read-only unlocks scale:** a block device has no locking. Multi-attach is normally limited because concurrent writers corrupt each other. Remove writers entirely and that limit disappears.

**The arithmetic:** 1.2 TB/s across 2,500 nodes is roughly 480 MB/s per node, with no per-node copy of the data to stage first.

**Storage pools fix cost, not speed:** when every disk is provisioned alone, each is sized for its own peak, and idle capacity and performance scatter across the fleet. A pool lets many disks draw on one bulk purchase. That is the same motivation behind disaggregated storage: stop stranding resources.

**The direction of travel:** both features move block storage away from one disk for one VM, toward storage shaped around whole fleets.

quiz.q: Your team wants 2,500 training nodes to share one Hyperdisk ML volume and also write checkpoints to it. Why won't this work as planned?
quiz.a: Hyperdisk ML reaches 2,500 instances only because they attach read-only. Writers would need coordination a block device doesn't provide. Checkpoints need separate writable storage.

mcq.q: What makes it safe for Hyperdisk ML to attach one volume to up to 2,500 instances?
options: Every instance attaches the volume read-only
Each instance gets its own private copy
A distributed lock manager serialises writes
The volume is replicated across two zones
mcq.why: With no writers, there is nothing to coordinate. A block device has no locking, which is what normally limits multi-attach.

section: 4.3 Google Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk and Azure Managed Disks
hook: Azure lets you give a database more IOPS for a batch window, then take them back. No migration. Which disk?
title: Azure's five disk types, from 400,000 IOPS down to HDD
body: Buying disk performance can mean buying capacity you never use. Azure's five Managed Disk types show three answers. **Premium SSD** (20,000 IOPS, 900 MB/s) ties performance to size tier, so you buy gigabytes to get speed. **Premium SSD v2** (80,000 IOPS, 2,000 MB/s) provisions it separately, with 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline free. **Ultra Disk** (400,000 IOPS, 10,000 MB/s) lets you change performance at runtime. Standard SSD and Standard HDD cover dev and backup.
takeaway: Size-tied performance makes you buy disk you don't need.
deeper:
**Size-tied:** Premium SSD is the older model, like AWS gp2. To get more IOPS you move up a size tier, buying capacity you may not need.

**Provisioned:** Premium SSD v2 is the newer model, like AWS gp3. Its free baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s makes small volumes useful without paying for performance.

**Changeable at runtime:** the table notes this for Ultra Disk. A database can get more IOPS for a heavy batch window and scale back afterwards without migrating data.

**Budget tiers:** Standard SSD (6,000 IOPS, 750 MB/s) for web servers and development, Standard HDD (2,000-3,000 IOPS, 500 MB/s) for backups and non-critical data. Ultra and Premium SSD v2 reach 64 TiB, the rest 32 TiB.

**The unit trap:** Azure quotes throughput in MB/s, AWS in MiB/s. Premium SSD v2's 2,000 MB/s is not the same number as gp3's 2,000 MiB/s. Pick redundancy, LRS or ZRS, as a separate decision.

quiz.q: A small database needs 15,000 IOPS but only 200 GiB. On Azure, why might Premium SSD v2 beat Premium SSD?
quiz.a: Premium SSD ties performance to size tier, so you would buy a much bigger disk to reach the IOPS. Premium SSD v2 provisions IOPS separately from capacity.

mcq.q: Which of these disk types ties performance to its size tier?
options: Premium SSD
Premium SSD v2
Ultra Disk
Google Hyperdisk Balanced
mcq.why: Premium SSD follows the older size-tied model, like AWS gp2. Premium SSD v2, Ultra Disk and Hyperdisk provision performance separately.

section: 4.3 Google Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk and Azure Managed Disks
hook: Azure offers 11 nines in one datacenter, or 12 nines across three zones. What do you pay for the extra nine?

predict.q: Azure ZRS disks replicate across three zones for 12 nines of durability. What is the main cost?
options: Higher write latency
Lower read throughput
No snapshot support

title: Azure's 12th nine costs you write latency
body: Three copies in one datacenter protect against a dead disk, not a dead building. Azure makes the choice explicit. **LRS** writes synchronously to three copies in one datacenter, stated at 11 nines. **ZRS** replicates synchronously across three availability zones, stated at 12 nines, at the cost of higher write latency. ZRS is supported only on Premium SSD and Standard SSD. A ZRS disk can be force-detached from a VM in a failed zone and attached to one in another zone.
takeaway: Every synchronous copy in another zone is a trip every write must take.
deeper:
**Why writes get slower:** synchronous replication means a write is acknowledged only after copies in other zones have it. That adds network distance to every write, and a database's commit rate is bounded by storage round-trip time.

**Why recovery gets easier:** if a zone fails, force-detach the ZRS disk from the dead VM and attach it to a VM in a healthy zone. The data comes back without restoring a backup or promoting an application replica.

**The restriction:** ZRS is supported only on Premium SSD and Standard SSD. Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2, the fastest tiers, need application-level replication for zone resilience.

**Read the fine print:** Azure states LRS at 11 nines, while AWS states most EBS types at 99.8-99.9%. Providers state durability very differently, so compare scope and definition, not just the digits.

quiz.q: Your latency-sensitive database runs on Azure Ultra Disk and must survive a zone failure. Why can't you just switch the disk to ZRS?
quiz.a: ZRS is supported only on Premium SSD and Standard SSD. On Ultra Disk, zone resilience must come from database replicas in other zones.

mcq.q: What can you do with a ZRS disk when its VM's zone fails?
options: Force-detach it and attach it in another zone
Restore it from an automatic hourly snapshot
Promote its LRS copy in the same datacenter
Nothing until the failed zone recovers
mcq.why: ZRS keeps synchronous copies in three zones, so the disk can be force-detached from the dead VM and attached to a VM elsewhere.

section: 4.3 Google Persistent Disk / Hyperdisk and Azure Managed Disks
hook: Three rival clouds built nearly the same disk. One of them left out a feature the other two made standard.
title: Three clouds built one disk, and AWS left out zones
body:
AWS, Google and Azure converged on one product shape: SSD volumes with independently provisioned IOPS and throughput, a high-end tier near or below 0.5 ms, and optional **cross-zone replication**, such as Google Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability and Azure ZRS.

The exception: AWS EBS volumes stay single-AZ. AWS pushes cross-AZ durability to the application or to its managed databases.
takeaway: On every cloud, decide which layer owns surviving a zone. Then write it down.
deeper:
**Why the shape converged:** workloads saturate different dimensions, so IOPS and throughput became separate knobs. A database's commit rate is bounded by storage latency, so every cloud has a sub-millisecond tier. Some data must survive a zone loss, so cross-zone replication appears.

**The trade AWS sidesteps:** synchronous cross-zone replication adds write latency, as Azure states for ZRS. On AWS, zone resilience comes instead from database replicas in other AZs or from managed databases.

**The portability trap:** a runbook that recovers from a zone loss by force-detaching an Azure ZRS disk and attaching it elsewhere has no EBS equivalent. On AWS, the same outage needs an application replica already running in another AZ.

**The senior question:** whatever the cloud, name the layer that owns cross-zone durability, the disk or the application, and design the recovery path around it before the outage.

quiz.q: You're porting a runbook from Azure to AWS. It recovers from zone loss by moving the ZRS disk to a VM in another zone. What must change?
quiz.a: EBS volumes are single-AZ and cannot move zones. On AWS you need a database replica already running in another AZ, or a managed database, to survive the zone loss.

mcq.q: Which block-storage feature do Google and Azure offer that AWS EBS does not?
options: Synchronous replication across zones
Independently provisioned IOPS and throughput
A high-end tier near 0.5 ms latency
SSD-backed volume types
mcq.why: Hyperdisk Balanced HA and Azure ZRS replicate across zones, while EBS stays single-AZ. The other features are common to all three clouds.

hook: The fastest disk on your cloud instance costs nothing extra. It also forgets everything at the worst moment.

predict.q: Your AWS instance keeps data on local NVMe instance store. Which event leaves that data intact?
options: A reboot
Stopping the instance
Hibernating the instance

title: Local NVMe: tens of µs, already paid for, gone on stop
body:
Network volumes pay for a network hop on every I/O. **Instance store** on AWS, or local SSD on Google and Azure, is NVMe flash physically inside the host. Latency is tens of microseconds instead of hundreds. IOPS and throughput are not capped by a per-volume product limit or instance EBS bandwidth, and the cost is included in the instance price.

The catch: data is **ephemeral**. It survives a reboot but not a stop, hibernate, terminate or disk failure. There is no snapshot and no detach.
takeaway: Local flash is exactly as durable as one machine.
deeper:
**The loss list, on AWS:** instance store data is lost when the instance stops, hibernates or terminates, or when the underlying disk fails. The last one needs no operator mistake. Hardware failure alone destroys the data.

**Why it is so fast:** Little's Law says IOPS = queue depth / latency. At tens of microseconds per I/O, even a shallow queue yields huge IOPS. A single commit stream that tops out near 2,000 commits per second at 0.5 ms network latency can go much higher.

**What you give up:** a network volume can be detached from a failed VM and attached elsewhere in minutes. Local NVMe cannot move, so a failed host means rebuilding from somewhere else.

**The real question:** the trade is speed and included cost against single-machine durability. Whether that is a bargain depends on whether the application already keeps copies elsewhere.

quiz.q: An engineer stops an EC2 instance overnight to save money, planning to restart it in the morning. Its database lives on instance store. What happens?
quiz.a: The data is gone. Instance store survives a reboot but is lost when the instance stops, hibernates or terminates. There is no snapshot or detach to recover it.

mcq.q: Why is local NVMe latency tens of microseconds rather than hundreds?
options: There is no network hop to storage
It uses a larger block size than EBS
It skips the filesystem journal entirely
The page cache is disabled by default
mcq.why: Instance store is flash physically inside the host, so each I/O avoids the network round trip that network block storage pays.

hook: Your NoSQL cluster keeps three copies across three zones, on disks that keep their own. What did that buy?
title: Pay for durability once: go local when the app replicates
body: Durability can live in the storage or in the application. Putting it in both costs twice. The rule big companies follow: use local NVMe when the application already replicates its own data. If the software keeps three copies across three zones, a lost node is just a replica to rebuild. A replicated network volume underneath means paying for durability twice, plus network latency on every I/O. Cassandra and ScyllaDB fit: they replicate at the application level and are sensitive to tail latency.
takeaway: Durability belongs in one layer. A second layer buys latency, not safety.
deeper:
**Why doubling is waste:** a replicated volume protects against a failed disk or server. An application with replicas in three zones already survives that, and a zone loss too. The volume's copies add cost and a network hop without covering a failure the app does not already handle.

**Easier still, caches:** flash caches such as Meta's CacheLib do not need durability at all. The source of truth lives elsewhere, and a lost cache is refilled.

**The flip side:** without application-level replication, local NVMe for a database is a data-loss incident waiting for a host failure.

**The number that decides:** even with replicas, compute rebuild time, how long you run with one fewer replica after losing a node. That, more often than the IOPS benchmark, settles local versus network.

quiz.q: A team runs ScyllaDB with three replicas across zones on replicated network volumes, and complains about p99 latency. What would you suggest, and why?
quiz.a: Move to local NVMe. ScyllaDB already replicates across zones, so the volumes duplicate durability and add a network hop to every I/O, which hurts tail latency. Check rebuild time first.

mcq.q: When does local NVMe usually make sense for a data store?
options: When the application already replicates its own data
When the database runs as a single node
When the data must survive the host failing
When volumes must be detached and moved
mcq.why: If the app keeps copies on other nodes, a lost disk is one replica to rebuild, so replicated network volumes would pay for durability twice.

hook: Kafka's own docs tell you to leave fsync off. Reckless, or does Kafka know something your database doesn't?
title: Kafka turns fsync off and still keeps your data
body:
Most databases treat fsync as the line between safe and lost. Kafka's documentation says the opposite: "durability in Kafka does not require syncing data to disk, as a failed node will always recover from its replicas." It recommends leaving application fsync off and relying on replication.

If a broker crashes with unflushed data in its page cache, it recovers by copying from its peers. Durability lives across machines, not on one disk. That design fits fast, cheap local NVMe.
takeaway: fsync protects one disk. Replicas protect the data.
deeper:
**The mirror image:** PostgreSQL relies on the local write-ahead log being on disk for committed transactions. For it, fsync is the durability boundary, and an fsync failure is fatal. Both are right, because each knows where its durability lives.

**Why forcing fsync would not help Kafka:** a message is safe once replicas on other brokers have it. Syncing every write locally would slow the system without protecting against a failure the replicas do not already cover.

**Filesystem advice, same docs:** XFS gave much better append latency than the best ext4 setup in Kafka's tests, 160 ms versus 250 ms+ for "Request Local Time" in a heavy test, with less variation and no special tuning.

**The catch:** the ext4 mount options that make ext4 fast, such as `data=writeback`, are unsafe on power loss.

quiz.q: A new Kafka operator enables fsync on every write 'to be safe', and throughput drops. Did they gain much durability?
quiz.a: Little, if replication is healthy. Kafka's durability comes from replicas on other brokers: a failed node recovers from them. Local fsync slows writes without being the source of durability.

mcq.q: Why does Kafka's documentation say durability does not require syncing to disk?
options: A failed node recovers its data from replicas
Kafka writes with O_DIRECT, bypassing the cache
XFS flushes appended data on every write
Brokers keep a battery-backed write cache
mcq.why: Kafka's durability comes from copies on other brokers, so data lost from one node's page cache is recovered from its peers.

hook: Local NVMe forgets everything when its host dies. In 2025, one company moved MySQL onto it anyway.
title: PlanetScale Metal: local NVMe cut MySQL p99 up to 65%

stat.label: best-case drop in p99 query latency

body:
Local NVMe is ephemeral, which makes it sound like the wrong home for MySQL. In March 2025, **PlanetScale** launched PlanetScale Metal, running MySQL through **Vitess** on locally attached NVMe instead. It reported up to a 65% drop in p99 query latency for workloads that moved.

Durability comes from database replication, not the disk. Vitess runs each shard with replicas, so a lost local disk is one replica to rebuild.
takeaway: Once the database replicates, the disk only needs to be fast.
deeper:
**Why p99 moved most:** p99 is the slowest 1% of queries, where a network storage path adds variability. Removing the network hop is exactly the change that should show up in the tail.

**Why it is safe:** the local-NVMe rule says use local disks when the application replicates its own data. Kafka and Cassandra are the classic cases, and Vitess extends the rule to sharded MySQL. A network volume under each replica would duplicate protection and add latency to every read and fsync.

**What does not go away:**
1. Rebuild time. Rebuilding a lost replica from a peer can take hours, and the shard runs with one fewer copy meanwhile.
2. Automation. Something must detect a lost local disk and rebuild the replica reliably.

**The lesson:** local versus network is about where durability lives, not whether the data is relational.

quiz.q: A team wants to copy PlanetScale's move and put their single-node PostgreSQL on local NVMe for the p99 win. What's missing?
quiz.a: Replication. PlanetScale's durability comes from database replicas, so a lost disk costs one replica. A single node on local NVMe loses its data when the host fails.
