mcq.q: Where does PlanetScale Metal get its durability, given that local NVMe is ephemeral?
options: From database replication across servers
From nightly snapshots of each NVMe disk
From RAID mirroring inside each host
From an EBS volume behind each disk
mcq.why: Vitess-managed MySQL keeps replicas on other servers, so losing one host's local disk means rebuilding one replica, not losing data.

hook: Local NVMe is faster and already paid for. So why do careful teams still put databases on network disks?

predict.q: A host dies. How long to get its data back: reattach its EBS volume, or rebuild 10 TB of local NVMe from a replica?
options: Minutes for EBS, hours for local
Hours for EBS, minutes for local
Minutes for both

title: Network disks reattach in minutes. Local rebuilds: hours.
body: Local NVMe dies with its host. That one fact gives network block storage three wins. First, single-node databases that cannot tolerate losing the node's data. Second, **fast recovery**: a failed VM's EBS volume can be attached to a new VM in minutes, while rebuilding 10 TB of local data from a replica can take hours. Third, **elastic capacity**: you can grow a network volume without changing instance type.
takeaway: The best disk for recovery is one that outlives its machine.
deeper:
**One root cause:** all three wins come from lifecycle independence. The volume is not tied to a host, so it survives host failure, moves to a replacement, and resizes on its own.

**Recovery, in numbers:** a 10 TB replica rebuilt over a 25 Gbps link, throttled to 40% to protect live traffic, runs at about 1.25 GB/s. That is 8,000 seconds, about 2.2 hours with one fewer replica. Reattaching a volume takes minutes, and the new node starts with its data present.

**Elasticity:** with local NVMe, running out of disk means moving to a larger instance type and migrating data, often paying for CPU and memory you do not need.

**The catch:** network volumes pay latency on every I/O. Weigh all three wins against local NVMe's speed and included cost, not against an IOPS benchmark.

quiz.q: Your dataset grows 30% a year on a single-node database using local NVMe. What two problems would a network volume avoid?
quiz.a: Losing all data when the host fails, since local NVMe dies with it, and forced instance-type changes to get more disk. A network volume grows without changing instance type.

mcq.q: Which situation favours network block storage over local NVMe?
options: A single-node database whose data must survive the host
A Cassandra cluster replicated across three zones
A flash cache that can be refilled from its source
A Kafka cluster relying on broker replication
mcq.why: Without application replicas, the node's data must outlive the node. Network volumes survive host failure; local NVMe does not.

hook: Your local NVMe replica just died with 10 TB on it. How long do you run one copy short?

predict.q: A 10 TB local replica rebuilds from a peer over a 25 Gbps link throttled to 40%. How long?
options: About 2.2 hours
About 10 minutes
About a day

title: 10 TB over a throttled 25 Gbps link: 2.2 hours exposed

stat.label: to rebuild 10 TB at 40% of a 25 Gbps link

body:
Local NVMe benchmarks look great until a node dies. Then its data must be copied back from a peer, and until the copy finishes you run with one fewer replica.

The math is short. A 25 Gbps link is about 3.1 GB/s. Throttle the rebuild to 40% to protect live traffic and you get about 1.25 GB/s. 10,000 GB divided by 1.25 GB/s is 8,000 seconds. That window, not the IOPS number, often decides local versus network.
takeaway: Before you buy the fast disk, price the slow rebuild.
deeper:
**Every input is a lever:** Rebuild time is data size divided by allowed rebuild bandwidth. Double the data per node and the window doubles. Raise the throttle and the window shrinks, but the rebuild starts competing with live traffic, which is the reason the throttle exists.

**What the window costs:** With three replicas, a 2.2-hour rebuild means 2.2 hours on two copies. The question is not only how long it takes, but whether running degraded for that long is acceptable for this data.

**The network contrast:** A failed VM's EBS volume can be attached to a new VM in minutes, with no bulk copy at all. Local disks trade that fast recovery for lower latency and included cost.

**The unit trap:** Links are quoted in bits, disks in bytes. 25 gigabits per second divided by 8 is about 3.1 gigabytes per second. Forget the divide-by-8 and your estimate is off by 8×.

quiz.q: Your team wants to double the data per node on a local-NVMe Cassandra cluster to save money. Rebuild bandwidth stays the same. What changes in the risk picture?
quiz.a: Rebuild time doubles, so after a node loss you run with one fewer replica twice as long. Check that the longer degraded window is still acceptable.

mcq.q: What number most often decides whether local NVMe is safe for a replicated database?
options: How long a lost node takes to rebuild from peers
The drive's peak IOPS in a synthetic benchmark
How many incremental snapshots the volume keeps
The per-volume throughput cap of the instance
mcq.why: While a node rebuilds you run one replica short. Rebuild time sets that exposure, so it often decides local versus network.

hook: Two teams pick the same database. One pays for durability twice, the other zero times. Which one gets paged?
title: Durability belongs in exactly one layer
body:
Storage debates usually start with benchmarks. The better first question is where durability lives. A replicating database on replicated network volumes pays for durability twice: once in money, and again in latency on every I/O. A database with no replica on local NVMe pays zero times, until the host fails.

The rule is to put durability in one layer, on purpose. If the app replicates, local NVMe is usually faster and cheaper. If it does not, use network volumes with snapshots.
takeaway: No replica on local NVMe is a data-loss incident waiting for a host failure.
deeper:
**The zero-layer trap:** Instance store data survives a reboot but is lost when the instance stops, hibernates or terminates, or when the disk fails. There is no snapshot and no detach. A database with no replica on it has no durability layer at all.

**The two-layer tax:** A network volume is itself replicated. Put Cassandra, which keeps three copies across three zones, on top of it and you pay for durability twice, plus network latency on every I/O.

**Why on purpose:** The layer must be chosen and written down. Otherwise a later cost cut, like dropping a replica, can silently remove the only durability you had. And EBS replicates only inside one AZ, so it is not a cross-zone layer either.

**The review question:** Ask the team to name the durability layer. If nobody can, there may be none.

quiz.q: A team runs single-replica PostgreSQL on local NVMe because benchmarks showed lower latency. What do you ask, and what are their two safe options?
quiz.a: Where does durability live? Right now nowhere: a host failure loses the data. Either add database replicas and keep local NVMe, or move to network volumes with snapshots.

mcq.q: A database keeps three replicas across three zones. Which storage choice follows the one-layer rule?
options: Local NVMe, letting the database's replication supply durability
Replicated network volumes under each of the three replicas
Local NVMe on the primary, network volumes on the replicas
Network volumes, with database replication turned off
mcq.why: The app already replicates, so it is the durability layer. Replicated volumes underneath pay for durability twice and add latency to every I/O.

hook: One server has idle SSDs and maxed-out CPUs. Its neighbour has the reverse. Neither can help the other.
title: Fixed SSDs per server strand flash or strand CPU
body:
Put 8 SSDs in every server and you lock in one ratio of CPU to flash. A CPU-bound service leaves its flash stranded. A data-heavy service fills its flash while cores sit idle.

**Disaggregation** breaks the ratio. Storage moves to its own machines and is served over the network, so compute and flash scale separately and every workload draws from one pool. Utilization goes up. The price is network latency on every I/O and a new failure domain.
takeaway: Pooling cures stranded hardware by adding a network, which becomes your next problem.
deeper:
**Why stranding adds up:** Workloads rarely need CPU and storage in the exact ratio a server ships with. Across a large fleet, every mismatched server leaves flash or cores unused, and that waste is paid for in hardware.

**What pooling buys:** Compute nodes and storage nodes are sized and bought separately. Any compute node can draw capacity from the pool, so the fleet runs closer to full.

**The two costs:** First, latency: every I/O now crosses a network instead of a local PCIe bus. Second, a new failure domain: the storage pool and the network can fail on their own, and one failure can hit many compute nodes at once. That is why blast radius matters so much in systems like EBS.

**Shrinking the penalty:** NVMe over Fabrics and RDMA exist to make remote flash feel nearly local.

quiz.q: Your search service uses 20% of its local flash while the analytics service, on the same server model, is out of disk with idle cores. What do you propose, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Disaggregate: pool flash on storage nodes and serve it over the network, so each service takes the ratio it needs. Cost: added network latency and a new failure domain.

mcq.q: What is the main trade-off of disaggregating flash from compute?
options: Better utilization, paid for with network latency and a new failure domain
Lower latency, paid for with worse utilization across the fleet
Stronger durability, paid for with fewer snapshots and clones
Simpler operations, paid for with higher flash write amplification
mcq.why: Pooling ends stranded flash and CPU, but every I/O crosses a network and the pool can fail independently of compute.

hook: Your SSD sits in another chassis across the network. Your server still talks to it like a local drive. How?
title: NVMe-oF makes a remote SSD look almost local
body:
Pooled flash only pays off if reaching it is fast. Every protocol translation between the host and a remote SSD adds delay.

**NVMe over Fabrics** (NVMe-oF) carries the NVMe protocol itself across a network instead of only a local PCIe bus. It runs over RDMA, TCP or Fibre Channel. The host keeps the same command model whether the SSD is inside the box or in a remote chassis, and on a good network the added latency is small.
takeaway: Remote flash is only as fast as the network carrying it.
deeper:
**Same protocol, longer wire:** NVMe was built for flash, with many deep queues that map well to multi-core CPUs. Extending that same protocol over a network avoids translation layers between the host and a remote SSD.

**The transport matters:** RDMA lets network cards move data straight into memory without involving the remote CPU, giving the lowest latency. TCP runs on ordinary Ethernet and is easier to deploy, but costs more CPU and latency. Fibre Channel fits existing storage-area networks.

**The fine print:** The phrase 'on a good network' is doing work. Congestion and tail latency on the fabric erode the near-local illusion. AWS's SRD, which sprays packets across many paths to cut tail latency, and Pangu's move from 25 to 100 Gbps RDMA are examples of how much network investment fast remote storage involves.

**EBS does its own version:** Nitro presents a remote EBS volume to the guest as a local NVMe device.

quiz.q: Two teams deploy NVMe-oF. One uses RDMA on a lightly loaded fabric, the other TCP on a congested network. Why might only one see near-local latency?
quiz.a: RDMA skips the remote CPU and has the lowest latency. TCP costs more CPU and latency, and congestion adds tail latency. NVMe-oF is near-local only on a good network.

mcq.q: What does NVMe over Fabrics change about an NVMe SSD?
options: Its protocol can run over a network, not just a PCIe bus
It speaks a file protocol so many hosts can share it
It can erase single pages instead of whole blocks
It replicates each write to three drives before acking
mcq.why: NVMe-oF extends NVMe over RDMA, TCP or Fibre Channel, so a remote SSD looks almost local at a small latency cost.

hook: Each Meta server was stuck with the flash it shipped with. In 2016 Meta published a box built to end that.
title: Meta Lightning: 15 SSDs per tray, 30 with bifurcation
body:
Servers with built-in SSDs lock flash to CPU in one fixed ratio. Meta's stated goal was to scale flash across applications and tune the compute-to-storage ratio.

In 2016 it published **Lightning**, an NVMe **JBOF** (just a bunch of flash). One chassis holds 15 SSDs per tray, or 30 with PCIe bifurcation, and connects to a head node with PCIe cables. Flash becomes something you attach in bulk, sized to the workload rather than to the server.
takeaway: Put flash in its own box, and the flash-to-CPU ratio becomes a choice.
deeper:
**Drives without a brain:** A JBOF holds drives but little or no general-purpose compute. The head node, connected over PCIe cables, does the processing and serves the flash.

**Why 30 instead of 15:** PCIe bifurcation splits one wide PCIe link into several narrower ones. The same tray can then connect twice as many drives, trading bandwidth per drive for density.

**What it fixes:** Applications that need lots of flash relative to CPU get it without buying servers full of idle cores. That attacks stranding head-on.

**Meta uses both models:** Inside its own fleet, Meta runs local flash where latency matters most and disaggregated flash where utilization matters most. Public clouds make disaggregation the default because they gain utilization across millions of customers.

quiz.q: An ML team needs far more flash per core than your standard server offers. Using Lightning's idea, how do you serve them without buying idle CPUs?
quiz.a: Attach JBOF trays of SSDs to a head node over PCIe, sizing flash to the workload instead of accepting whatever ratio each server ships with.

mcq.q: What does PCIe bifurcation let a Lightning tray do?
options: Connect 30 SSDs instead of 15 by splitting wide PCIe links
Mirror each SSD's data to a second tray automatically
Serve its SSDs over RDMA to any server in the datacenter
Run storage software on the tray without a head node
mcq.why: Bifurcation splits a wide PCIe link into narrower ones, doubling drives per tray from 15 to 30 at lower bandwidth per drive.

hook: Fast SSDs, a fast RDMA network. What else stands between a cloud disk and 100-microsecond I/O?
title: Pangu kept 99.9% of cloud-disk I/Os under 1 ms

stat.label: P999 latency for Pangu's EBS cloud disk

body:
Pangu, in development since 2009, is Alibaba's unified storage platform under its Elastic Block Storage, object storage, NAS and PolarDB. Once SSDs and RDMA made the hardware fast, kernel data copies and interrupts became the delay.

A FAST 2023 paper describes Pangu 2.0 building a **user-space storage operating system** with a **run-to-completion** model: one thread carries each request start to finish. The target was 100-microsecond-level I/O.
takeaway: Once the hardware is fast, the kernel becomes the slow part.
deeper:
**Run-to-completion:** A thread takes a request and processes it all the way through, without handing it off or waiting on interrupts. That cuts both overhead and variability.

**Bigger pipes, less waste:** Pangu later moved storage servers from 25 Gbps to 100 Gbps RDMA and added techniques to reduce traffic amplification: the extra network traffic from replication and internal data movement beyond the user's own bytes.

**Why P999 matters:** P999 is the slowest 0.1% of I/Os, exactly where disaggregated storage usually suffers. Reporting it under 1 ms for the EBS cloud disk is a claim about the tail, not the average.

**One substrate, many products:** Like Google's block storage on Colossus, Pangu is a shared platform beneath several storage products rather than a dedicated block system.

quiz.q: Your storage server's SSDs and RDMA NICs are far from saturated, yet I/O latency is stuck well above 100 µs. Following Pangu 2.0, where do you look and what do you change?
quiz.a: The software path: kernel data copies, interrupts and handoffs. Move storage processing to user space with run-to-completion threads so each request goes straight through.

mcq.q: Why did Pangu 2.0 adopt a run-to-completion model in user space?
options: To avoid kernel data copies and interrupts on the I/O path
To replicate each write across three zones before acking
To let SSDs skip garbage collection during peak traffic
To move storage servers from RDMA back to plain TCP
mcq.why: With fast SSDs and RDMA, kernel copies and interrupts dominated latency. User-space run-to-completion removes them, aiming at 100-microsecond-level I/O.

hook: Every public cloud serves its disks over the network. Meta owns its hardware outright. Does it do the same?
title: Clouds pool their flash. Meta keeps some local.
body:
Public clouds make **disaggregation** the default: EBS, Persistent Disk and Pangu-backed EBS all serve volumes over the network. EBS on Nitro even presents a remote volume to the VM as local NVMe. The reason is scale: pooling across millions of customers keeps the hardware busy.

Meta does a different sum. It knows its own workloads, so it uses both: local flash where latency matters most, disaggregated flash where utilization matters most.
takeaway: Pool for utilization, go local for latency, and know which one you need.
deeper:
**Why clouds pool:** A provider sees huge variation in how much storage each VM wants. Pooling lets it sell exactly the capacity and performance each customer buys while keeping flash busy. It also powers the features people pay for: detach and reattach, snapshots, resizing, and data that outlives the host.

**Why Meta splits:** A company running its own fleet can put its most latency-critical services on local flash. Workloads where utilization and flexibility matter more go to pooled flash.

**Same rule, different scale:** This mirrors the local-versus-network choice for a single app. If the software replicates and needs low latency, go local. Otherwise pooled storage buys flexibility.

**The trade in one line:** Disaggregated flash trades a small latency cost for much better utilization.

quiz.q: You run a cloud and consider offering VMs only local NVMe, since it's faster. Why would that hurt the business?
quiz.a: You'd lose pooled utilization across millions of customers and the features they pay for: detach and reattach, snapshots, resizing and data that survives the host.

mcq.q: Why do public clouds make disaggregated storage the default?
options: Pooling flash across millions of customers raises utilization
Network volumes have lower latency than local NVMe flash
Local NVMe cannot be encrypted on shared cloud hardware
Disaggregation removes the need for replication entirely
mcq.why: Pooling flash across millions of customers keeps hardware busy and enables detach, snapshots and resizing, which outweighs a small latency cost.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
hook: Kafka's tests pitted the best-tuned ext4 against a filesystem left on defaults. The untuned one won.

predict.q: In Kafka's heavy-load tests, how did XFS compare with the best ext4 setup on append latency?
options: XFS was faster: about 160 ms vs 250 ms+
They were within a few percent of each other
ext4 won once tuned with data=writeback

title: Kafka's tests: XFS 160 ms, best ext4 250 ms+
body:
Kafka does heavy sequential appends across many partitions, so the filesystem shows up in latency. Both ext4 and XFS are **journaling** filesystems: they log metadata changes before applying them, so a crash doesn't corrupt the directory structure.

In Kafka's documented tests, XFS gave 160 ms 'Request Local Time' in a heavy test, versus 250 ms and more for the best ext4 setup, with less variation. XFS, designed for large files and parallel I/O, needed no special tuning.
takeaway: A mount option that buys speed is also a durability decision.
deeper:
**What journaling covers:** Before changing directory entries or allocation maps, the filesystem writes the intended change to a journal. After a crash it replays or discards entries to get back to a consistent structure. That protects metadata structure, not necessarily your file contents, so applications still need fsync.

**The ext4 trap:** The Kafka docs warn that the mount options that make ext4 fast, such as data=writeback, are unsafe on power loss. They relax ordering between data and metadata writes, so after a crash a file can point at garbage.

**Why it generalizes:** Kafka's workload looks like many log-structured systems. XFS delivered lower and steadier append latency without trading away safety.

**The review habit:** When someone proposes a performance mount option, ask what it does on power loss before asking how fast it is.

quiz.q: A colleague gets ext4 close to XFS's Kafka numbers by mounting with data=writeback. Why push back?
quiz.a: Kafka's docs warn that fast ext4 options like data=writeback are unsafe on power loss. XFS gets lower, steadier latency with no tuning and no durability risk.

mcq.q: What does a journaling filesystem like ext4 or XFS protect after a crash?
options: Metadata structure, so directories aren't corrupted
File contents, so fsync is no longer needed
Page-cache data, so power loss loses nothing
Replicas, so a failed disk rebuilds from peers
mcq.why: Journaling logs metadata changes before applying them, keeping the directory structure consistent after a crash. Durable file data still needs fsync.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
hook: write() returned success. A second later the power failed. Your data is gone, and nothing was buggy.
title: write() returning success doesn't mean it's on disk
body:
An app calls `write()`, gets success, and moves on. But by default write() only copies the data into the kernel's **page cache** in memory. The kernel writes it to disk later, when it chooses. Lose power before then and the data is gone.

To make data durable, the app calls `fsync()`. It forces the file's dirty pages and metadata to stable storage and waits until that is done. Only when fsync returns is the write safe.
takeaway: write() hands data to memory. fsync() hands it to the disk.
deeper:
**Why the cache exists:** Buffering writes in memory lets the kernel combine and reorder them and write efficiently in the background. Reads of recent data come straight from RAM. The price is a gap between what the app thinks it wrote and what is actually on disk.

**The vulnerable window:** Pages changed in memory but not yet written are called dirty pages. fsync closes the window for one file by flushing its dirty data and the metadata needed to find it, then blocking until storage confirms.

**Where it shows up:** A crash-consistent snapshot captures what is on the volume, not what is still in the page cache. That is why unflushed writes are missing after a restore.

**The bill:** Every fsync waits for at least one full storage round trip. That ties a database's commit rate directly to storage latency.

quiz.q: Your service writes each order to a file and tells the customer OK as soon as write() returns. A host loses power. What can go wrong, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: Orders still in the page cache never reached disk, so they vanish even though customers saw OK. Call fsync and reply only after it returns.

mcq.q: When is data written with write() safe against power loss?
options: After fsync() on the file returns
As soon as write() returns success
When the process closes the file
Once the page cache fills up
mcq.why: write() only copies data to the page cache. fsync() forces dirty pages and metadata to stable storage and waits until they are there.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
hook: Your volume has IOPS to spare, yet one commit stream won't go faster. The disk isn't busy. What's the limit?
title: 0.5 ms per fsync caps one commit stream at 2,000/s

stat.label: max commits/s per stream at 0.5 ms latency

body:
A commit is safe only after its **write-ahead log** (WAL) record is fsync'd, so every commit pays at least one storage round trip. At 0.5 ms network latency, one commit stream can do at most 1 / 0.0005 = 2,000 commits per second, however many IOPS you provisioned.

Databases answer with **group commit**: while one fsync is in flight, other transactions queue, and the next fsync flushes all their WAL records at once.
takeaway: Durability is paid in round trips, so share the round trip.
deeper:
**Little's Law again:** With one I/O outstanding at a time, the ceiling is one divided by latency. Commits in a single stream are exactly that: each must wait for its fsync before the next can finish.

**Two ways out:**
1. More parallelism. Group commit turns many commits into one I/O. Each commit waits slightly longer, but throughput rises sharply.
2. Lower latency. Local NVMe answers in tens of microseconds, so the ceiling is much higher. That is one reason latency-sensitive databases move to local disks.

**The benchmark trap:** Turn fsync off and commits finish at memory speed. The number looks spectacular and means nothing for production.

**The rule:** Databases live or die by fsync. Commit rate is bounded by fsync latency on the real storage, not by the IOPS on the invoice.

quiz.q: A DBA doubles the volume's provisioned IOPS, but a single-stream commit benchmark without group commit doesn't budge. Why, and what would actually help?
quiz.a: Each commit waits for one fsync round trip, so the ceiling is one divided by latency, not IOPS. Group commit or lower-latency storage such as local NVMe helps.

mcq.q: How does group commit raise a database's commit throughput?
options: Many transactions share one WAL fsync and its round trip
Commits skip fsync and let the page cache flush later
Each transaction gets its own fsync on a separate volume
The WAL is written in larger blocks to lift the IOPS cap
mcq.why: While one fsync is in flight, others queue. The next fsync flushes all their WAL records together, so one round trip covers many commits.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
hook: Your fsync failed, so you retried it. The retry succeeded. In 2018 PostgreSQL learned why that's no comfort.

predict.q: On Linux, an fsync fails. What did PostgreSQL decide in 2018 is the only safe response?
options: Crash and recover from the WAL
Retry the fsync until it succeeds
Log a warning and keep serving

title: The fsync retry that reports success on lost data
body:
The obvious way to handle a failed fsync is to retry it. In 2018 the PostgreSQL community found why that is dangerous on Linux. When a background write-back fails, the kernel can mark the pages clean and drop the data. A later fsync, maybe from another process, may not report the error.

PostgreSQL now treats an fsync failure as fatal: PANIC, then recover from the **write-ahead log**.
takeaway: After an fsync error, the page cache is a witness you can't trust.
deeper:
**Why the retry lies:** Once the kernel has marked the failed pages clean, it sees nothing dirty. A retried fsync has nothing to flush, so it returns success. The app believes its data is durable when it never reached disk.

**Why crashing is correct:** PostgreSQL relies on its local WAL being on disk for committed transactions. On restart it replays the WAL, rebuilding state from records it knows are durable, instead of trusting whatever the page cache holds.

**The long-term fix:** Kernel developers pointed to direct I/O. If data never sits in the page cache, the kernel cannot silently drop it after a failed write-back.

**The contrast:** Kafka relies on replicas, not local fsync, for durability, so the same kernel behavior matters far less to it.

quiz.q: Your storage service retries fsync up to three times on error and carries on if a retry succeeds. On Linux, why is that unsafe, and what should it do?
quiz.a: A failed write-back may have marked pages clean and dropped them, so a retry succeeds without writing anything. Treat the error as fatal: crash and recover from a durable log.

mcq.q: Why can a retried fsync succeed on Linux even though the data was lost?
options: The kernel marked the failed pages clean, leaving nothing to flush
The disk's write cache acknowledged the data a second time
The kernel replayed the WAL automatically before the retry
The retry was served by a replica that still held the data
mcq.why: After a failed background write-back, Linux can mark pages clean and drop the data, so the next fsync sees nothing dirty and reports success.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
hook: Your database caches its hot pages in RAM. So does the kernel. You're paying for the same memory twice.
title: O_DIRECT: stop caching the same page twice
body:
A database with its own **buffer pool** already decides which pages stay in memory. By default the kernel's page cache keeps a second copy of the same data, and the kernel also decides when writes reach disk.

With `O_DIRECT`, reads and writes skip the page cache and go straight to the device. Databases that manage their own buffer pool, as MySQL InnoDB is commonly configured, use it to avoid double caching and to control exactly when writes land.
takeaway: If you run your own cache, don't let the kernel keep a shadow copy.
deeper:
**Who knows better:** The database knows which index pages are hot and which belong to uncommitted transactions. The kernel doesn't. Letting both cache the same pages wastes memory and adds a second layer that decides when data is written.

**The fsync connection:** After PostgreSQL's 2018 fsync discovery, kernel developers pointed to direct I/O as the long-term answer. If data never sits in the page cache, the kernel cannot silently drop it after a failed write-back.

**The price:** The application takes on work the kernel used to do. It loses the kernel's readahead and write combining, so it must cache well and keep enough I/O in flight to reach the IOPS it paid for.

**Who shouldn't bother:** Software without a sophisticated buffer pool generally does better with the page cache.

quiz.q: A team switches a simple key-value store with no buffer pool to O_DIRECT, and reads get slower. Why?
quiz.a: It lost the kernel's page cache, readahead and write combining, and has no buffer pool of its own to replace them. Direct I/O pays off only with a real buffer pool.

mcq.q: Why is MySQL InnoDB commonly configured with O_DIRECT?
options: To avoid caching data twice and control when writes reach disk
To let the kernel merge its writes into larger sequential I/Os
To make every write durable without ever calling fsync
To share its buffer pool with other processes on the host
mcq.why: InnoDB manages its own buffer pool. O_DIRECT skips the kernel's page cache, so data isn't cached twice and the database controls write timing.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
hook: The staging benchmark looked spectacular, so you sized production from it. Launch day, commits crawl. Why?
title: An fsync-off benchmark measures memory, not your disk
body:
Turn fsync off, or let a write cache 'help', and a database benchmark produces a beautiful number. Size production from it and the plan fails under real load.

The benchmark skipped the storage round trip every real commit must pay, so it measured memory speed. With durability on, one commit stream at 0.5 ms network latency tops out near 2,000 commits per second before group commit. Always benchmark with the durability settings you will run.
takeaway: A performance number means nothing without the durability settings it was measured with.
deeper:
**Why it looks so good:** Without fsync, a commit completes as soon as the data is in memory. The benchmark never waits on storage, so its throughput says nothing about your disk.

**The write-cache version:** If a write cache acknowledges writes before they reach stable storage, the benchmark is fast but may not match the production storage path, and may not survive power loss.

**The same trap in filesystems:** Kafka's docs warn that ext4 options like data=writeback, which make ext4 fast, are unsafe on power loss. Speed bought by relaxing durability is a loan against the next crash.

**How the gap shows up:** A plan sized on the inflated figure provisions far too few servers. Nobody notices until production traffic arrives, which is the worst possible time to find out.

quiz.q: A vendor's benchmark shows huge commit rates, measured with fsync disabled. You will run with fsync on network storage at 0.5 ms. How do you estimate your real ceiling?
quiz.a: One commit stream is capped near 1 / 0.0005 = 2,000 commits per second. Group commit raises that. Rerun the benchmark with your real durability settings to be sure.

mcq.q: Why does a benchmark run with fsync disabled overstate production commit rates?
options: It skips the storage round trip that every real commit pays
It overloads the page cache and slows reads down instead
It forces group commit, which production databases avoid
It measures IOPS instead of throughput on the same volume
mcq.why: Without fsync, commits finish at memory speed. In production each commit waits for a WAL fsync, so throughput is bounded by storage latency.

hook: Kubernetes heals a crashed pod by starting a new one on any node. For a database, that's the problem.
title: Kubernetes restarts pods anywhere. Data lives in one place.
body:
Kubernetes was built for stateless pods: kill one, start another anywhere. That freedom powers bin packing, rolling upgrades and self-healing.

Storage breaks the model, because data lives in one place. A database pod must be reunited with its own volume, which may be zonal, like an EBS volume stuck in one AZ, or tied to one node's local NVMe. Kubernetes answers with a stack of abstractions: claims, classes, CSI drivers, StatefulSets and operators.
takeaway: The scheduler's freedom ends where the data lives.
deeper:
**What each piece solves:**
1. PVCs and StorageClasses separate what an app asks for from how storage is provided.
2. CSI drivers connect Kubernetes to real storage systems.
3. WaitForFirstConsumer keeps a new volume in the pod's zone.
4. StatefulSets give pods stable identities that map to stable volumes.
5. Operators encode database operations Kubernetes knows nothing about.

**Why moving is hard:** Moving a network volume to a new node takes time, and a stuck detach can block the new pod for minutes. A zonal volume cannot follow a pod to another zone at all. With local disks, losing the node can mean losing that replica's data.

**The bottom line:** Databases on Kubernetes work, but their failure modes differ from stateless apps and have to be designed for.

quiz.q: A stateless web pod and a database pod both crash on a node in zone A. Why can the web pod restart anywhere while the database pod may be stuck?
quiz.a: The web pod carries no data. The database pod must reattach its own volume, which may be zonal or local to that node, so it cannot simply start anywhere.

mcq.q: Why does persistent storage clash with Kubernetes' original design?
options: Pods were meant to restart anywhere, but data lives in one place
Containers cannot write to block devices without a host filesystem
The scheduler cannot place more than one pod on a storage node
Stateful pods need more CPU than the scheduler can reserve
mcq.why: Kubernetes assumes a failed pod can start on any node. A stateful pod must reach its specific volume, which may be tied to a zone or a node.

hook: Your app asks for 100 GiB of fast disk and never learns if it got EBS or an NFS share. That's deliberate.
title: PVC is the request, PV is the disk, bound 1:1
body:
An app shouldn't need to know which cloud it runs on, so Kubernetes splits storage in two. A **PersistentVolume** (PV) is real storage: an EBS volume, a Persistent Disk, a local disk, an NFS share. A **PersistentVolumeClaim** (PVC) is a request: 'I need 100 GiB, ReadWriteOnce, class fast-ssd'.

The control plane binds each claim to one PV, one-to-one. Pods mount the claim, never the disk directly.
takeaway: Ask for what you need, not for where it lives.
deeper:
**Think hotel booking:** The PVC is the reservation: size, access mode, class. The PV is the room. The control plane is the front desk, assigning exactly one room per reservation, and the pod gets in by showing the reservation. Two unrelated guests never share a room by accident.

**Why data outlives pods:** A PV's lifecycle is independent of any pod. A pod can die and be replaced, and the replacement mounts the same PVC, so it finds the same data.

**What happens at checkout:** Deleting the claim triggers the PV's reclaim policy. Delete removes the cloud volume. Retain keeps it for manual cleanup.

**The same shape again:** Snapshots copy the pattern. A VolumeSnapshot is the request, like a PVC, and a VolumeSnapshotContent is the actual snapshot, like a PV.

quiz.q: A pod using a PVC is deleted and recreated on another node in the same zone. Does it get its data back? Why?
quiz.a: Yes. The PV's lifecycle is independent of the pod and the claim stays bound to it, so the new pod mounts the same PVC and reaches the same volume.

mcq.q: What does a PersistentVolumeClaim describe?
options: A request for storage by size, access mode and class
The actual cloud disk and its provider-specific ID
The driver that formats and mounts the volume
A point-in-time copy of an existing volume
mcq.why: A PVC is the user's request. The control plane binds it one-to-one to a PV, the real storage, so apps stay portable across backends.

hook: Nobody created a disk this morning. Yet a new EBS volume appeared, sized and tuned for your database.
title: Name a StorageClass and a matching volume appears
body:
Pre-creating disks means guessing sizes ahead of time and making users wait. A **StorageClass** describes a kind of storage, which provisioner creates it, and with what parameters, for example EBS gp3 with 6,000 IOPS.

With **dynamic provisioning**, when a PVC names a StorageClass and no PV matches, the provisioner creates a new volume on demand. Storage becomes self-service: write a claim, get a disk.
takeaway: Encode storage decisions once, in the class, not in every claim.
deeper:
**A production class, line by line:** The db-gp3 example uses provisioner ebs.csi.aws.com and packs several good choices into one object:
1. type gp3 with iops 6000 and throughput 500 (MiB/s), set separately.
2. reclaimPolicy: Retain, so deleting the claim keeps the cloud volume.
3. volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer, so the volume is created in the pod's zone.
4. allowVolumeExpansion: true, so claims can grow later.

**Why separate knobs matter:** gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput independently of capacity, so the class buys performance without buying a bigger disk.

**Many classes, one cluster:** A cluster usually offers several classes, such as a cheap general one and a fast one for databases. Each PVC picks one by name, and the platform team controls what each name means.

quiz.q: A team's PVC names class db-gp3 and no PV exists yet. Walk through what happens before the pod can use the disk.
quiz.a: WaitForFirstConsumer holds creation until the pod is scheduled. Then the EBS CSI provisioner creates a gp3 volume in that zone, a PV is bound to the claim, and the disk is mounted.

mcq.q: What happens when a PVC names a StorageClass and no existing PV matches?
options: The class's provisioner creates a new volume on demand
The PVC waits until an admin creates a matching PV
The PVC binds to the largest free PV in the cluster
Kubernetes shares an existing PV with the new claim
mcq.why: That is dynamic provisioning: the provisioner creates a volume matching the class's parameters, so nobody has to pre-create disks.

hook: ReadWriteOnce sounds like one writer. Two database pods can still write the same volume at the same time.

predict.q: Two pods on the same node mount one ReadWriteOnce volume read-write. What happens?
options: It's allowed: the limit is per node, not per pod
Kubernetes blocks the second pod from starting
The volume turns read-only for both pods

title: ReadWriteOnce means one node, not one pod
body:
A block volume has no coordination between writers, so two machines writing it independently would corrupt the filesystem. Access modes guard against that.

**ReadWriteOnce**: read-write from one node. ReadOnlyMany: many nodes, read-only. ReadWriteMany: many nodes read-write, usually a shared filesystem. **ReadWriteOncePod**: exactly one pod. The catch is that ReadWriteOnce counts nodes, so two pods on the same node can both mount it. For a database, pick the strictest mode.
takeaway: Pick the most restrictive access mode your workload allows.
deeper:
**Why block means once:** A cloud block volume like EBS is a raw array of blocks with no coordination between writers. That is why such volumes are typically ReadWriteOnce.

**Where Many comes from:** ReadWriteMany workloads, such as a shared content directory, are usually backed by managed network filesystems like Amazon EFS, Google Filestore or Azure Files. They handle POSIX semantics across many clients, but metadata operations are much slower than on a local disk.

**Why OncePod exists:** A database must never have two instances writing the same data files. ReadWriteOnce stops a second node but not a second pod on the same node. ReadWriteOncePod closes that gap.

**ReadOnlyMany's niche:** Distributing static data, such as a reference dataset, to many nodes at once.

quiz.q: A developer wants a ReadWriteMany EBS-backed volume so 10 web pods can share uploads. What do you tell them?
quiz.a: A block volume like EBS is typically ReadWriteOnce; independent writers would corrupt it. ReadWriteMany needs a shared filesystem such as EFS, Filestore or Azure Files.

mcq.q: Which access mode guarantees that only one pod can mount a volume read-write?
options: ReadWriteOncePod
ReadWriteOnce
ReadOnlyMany
ReadWriteMany
mcq.why: ReadWriteOnce limits a volume to one node, so two pods there could both write. ReadWriteOncePod restricts it to exactly one pod.

hook: You delete a PVC. Does the cloud disk behind it, and your data, go too? One rarely noticed field decides.
title: Retain: the field that keeps a deleted claim's data
body:
Kubernetes makes cleanup cascade. Delete a PVC and something has to decide what happens to the cloud disk behind it. That something is the **reclaim policy**. With `Delete`, the cloud volume is removed along with the claim. With `Retain`, the volume stays for manual cleanup, so the data outlives the claim.

For production databases, `Retain` is often the safer choice. A mistaken claim deletion, or a whole namespace wiped by accident, then costs you some objects instead of the data.
takeaway: Make deleting data a deliberate human act, never a side effect.
deeper:
**Where Delete fits:** Test clusters and preview environments clean up after themselves, and nobody pays for orphaned disks. That same convenience is the danger in production.

**The cascade:** A `kubectl delete namespace` can remove every PVC in it. Under `Delete`, each PVC takes its cloud volume along, and the database goes with it. `Retain` breaks the chain at the volume: Kubernetes objects can be recreated, but the disk stays until someone removes it on purpose.

**The cost:** Retained volumes are housekeeping. Someone has to track them and clean them up, or they keep accruing charges.

**Not the whole plan:** Retain is one layer. Pair it with deletion protection and off-cluster backups, because a mistake bigger than one namespace can still reach volumes and snapshots inside the same cluster or account. The example db-gp3 StorageClass sets `reclaimPolicy: Retain` for exactly this reason.

quiz.q: An engineer cleans up what they think is a staging namespace, but the prod context is selected. The prod StorageClass uses Delete. What is lost, and which setting would have saved the disks?
quiz.a: Every PVC in the namespace and, through the Delete policy, their cloud volumes and data. With reclaimPolicy Retain, the volumes would have survived for recovery.

mcq.q: A PVC bound to a PV with reclaim policy Retain is deleted. What happens to the cloud volume?
options: It stays until someone removes it manually
It is deleted along with the claim
It is snapshotted and then deleted
It is rebound to the next matching claim
mcq.why: Retain keeps the underlying volume after its claim is gone, so the data survives until a human deliberately cleans it up.

hook: Your PVC is bound, your nodes have spare CPU, and the database pod stays Pending forever. Why?

predict.q: A database pod stays Pending forever, though its PVC is bound and the cluster has spare CPU. Likeliest cause?
options: The volume was created in a different zone than the pod
The volume's provisioned IOPS are too low
The reclaim policy is set to Retain

title: Create the disk before the pod, and you strand the pod
body:
A zonal EBS volume can only attach to a node in its own zone. With **Immediate binding**, the provisioner creates the volume as soon as the PVC appears, before the scheduler has looked at the pod. If the pod then lands in zone B and the volume sits in zone A, the pod can never start.

**WaitForFirstConsumer** flips the order: schedule the pod first, then create the volume in that pod's zone.
takeaway: Let the scheduler pick the place first. The disk follows the pod.
deeper:
**Why order matters:** The scheduler weighs CPU, memory, node affinity and anti-affinity with other replicas. Immediate binding picks the volume's zone before any of that. A zonal block volume cannot move to another Availability Zone, so a mismatch is permanent for that pod: it cannot run where the volume is if that zone lacks room, and it cannot use the volume anywhere else.

**The fixed sequence:**
1. The PVC names a StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer.
2. The pod is scheduled onto a node.
3. The provisioner creates the volume in that node's zone.
4. The PV binds and the pod starts.

**Same logic, one level down:** The Kubernetes docs recommend WaitForFirstConsumer for local persistent volumes too, where the constraint is a node instead of a zone.

**The cost of forgetting:** One missing line in a StorageClass, and stateful pods fail to start at random, depending on where the scheduler happened to put them.

quiz.q: Two StorageClasses differ only in binding mode. Pods on class A sometimes hang in Pending; pods on class B never do. Which uses Immediate, and why does it fail only sometimes?
quiz.a: Class A. Immediate picks the volume's zone before scheduling, so it fails only when the scheduler happens to place the pod in a different zone.

mcq.q: What does volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer change?
options: The volume is created after the pod is scheduled, in its zone
The pod waits until the volume's first snapshot completes
The volume is replicated to every zone before binding
The first pod to claim the volume gets exclusive access
mcq.why: It delays volume creation until a pod is scheduled, so a zonal volume lands in the same zone as the pod that needs it.

hook: Kubernetes once compiled storage vendors' plugins into its own code. What got them out?
title: CSI: storage drivers moved out of Kubernetes itself
body:
Before CSI, storage plugins were compiled into Kubernetes itself. The **Container Storage Interface** is a standard API between orchestrators and storage systems, so each vendor now ships a **CSI driver** that runs as pods: the EBS CSI driver, the GCE PD driver, Ceph's driver.

Each driver splits in two. The controller part creates, deletes, attaches and snapshots volumes through the cloud API. The node part formats and mounts the device on the host.
takeaway: Call the cloud API once, centrally. Touch the disk on the host that uses it.
deeper:
**Why split it:** Cloud API calls can happen once, from anywhere. Formatting and mounting must happen on the specific host where the pod runs. The controller/node split follows that line.

**The full path for a 100Gi PVC of class db-gp3:**
1. The StorageClass names the provisioner `ebs.csi.aws.com`.
2. With WaitForFirstConsumer, the pod is scheduled first.
3. The CSI controller calls the cloud API to create an EBS volume in the pod's zone, and the PV binds to the PVC.
4. The volume is attached to the chosen node through the cloud API.
5. The node plugin formats it if needed and mounts it, and the container sees it at /var/lib/db.

**A diagram trap:** Some flow diagrams label the node plugin "attach, format, mount". In CSI, attach is a controller job; the node plugin stages and mounts.

**What else rides on CSI:** Kubernetes volume snapshots work only with CSI drivers.

quiz.q: A new volume was created and shows as attached to the right node, but the container cannot see its data directory. Which half of the CSI driver do you debug first?
quiz.a: The node plugin. Create and attach are controller jobs done through the cloud API; formatting and mounting the device on the host belong to the node part.

mcq.q: In a CSI driver, which part attaches a new EBS volume to a node?
options: The controller part, through the cloud API
The node plugin, running on that host
The kubelet, with a compiled-in EBS plugin
The StorageClass, when the claim is bound
mcq.why: The controller part handles create, delete, attach and snapshot through the cloud API. The node part only formats and mounts on the host.

hook: Your CSI driver works and the snapshot request applied cleanly, yet no snapshot ever appears. What's missing?
title: Kubernetes snapshots need a controller you install
body:
Kubernetes models snapshots as **CRDs**, not core types. They work only with CSI drivers and need a snapshot controller installed. Without the controller, nothing acts on your request.

The objects mirror the volume trio. A **VolumeSnapshot** is the user's request, like a PVC. A VolumeSnapshotContent is the actual snapshot, like a PV. A VolumeSnapshotClass holds driver parameters, like a StorageClass. Snapshots are crash-consistent by default, and a new PVC can be created from one or cloned from another PVC.
takeaway: A request is only as good as the controller that answers it.
deeper:
**Why mirror PV and PVC:** Users ask for a snapshot without knowing how the backend takes one. The driver produces a real snapshot object bound to that request, the same way a PV binds to a PVC.

**Crash-consistent by default:** The snapshot captures volume blocks at one instant, like a power cut. Data still in the page cache is missing. A database restored from it replays its write-ahead log, as after a crash. For application consistency, freeze the filesystem or have the database checkpoint first, a step an operator can coordinate.

**What you can build:** A new PVC can be created from a snapshot, or cloned straight from another PVC. That covers restoring after a bad migration or standing up a copy of production data for testing.

**The limit:** Everything here depends on the CSI driver. Storage without one gets no Kubernetes snapshots at all.

quiz.q: A team restores a PostgreSQL PVC from a default Kubernetes snapshot. The database spends a while in recovery, then serves traffic. Is the data corrupted? What happened?
quiz.a: No. The snapshot was crash-consistent, like a power cut. PostgreSQL replayed its write-ahead log to reach a consistent state; only writes still in the page cache are missing.

mcq.q: Which Kubernetes snapshot object plays the role a PV plays for volumes?
options: VolumeSnapshotContent
VolumeSnapshot
VolumeSnapshotClass
PersistentVolumeClaim
mcq.why: VolumeSnapshotContent is the actual snapshot, like a PV. VolumeSnapshot is the request, like a PVC, and VolumeSnapshotClass holds driver parameters.

hook: A database pod dies and Kubernetes replaces it. How does the brand-new pod find the dead one's data?
title: db-1 dies, db-1 comes back, with the same disk
body:
A normal Deployment treats pods as interchangeable, with random names and no disk of their own. Database replicas are not interchangeable. Each holds its own copy of the data at a known address.

A **StatefulSet** gives each pod a stable name (db-0, db-1, db-2), a stable network identity, and its own PVC from a **volumeClaimTemplate**. If db-1 dies, the replacement is also db-1 and reattaches the same PVC. Pods are created and updated in order, and deleting or scaling down keeps the PVCs by default.
takeaway: Give a replica a stable name and its own disk, and death becomes a restart.
deeper:
**Why stable identity:** db-0 may be the primary and db-1 and db-2 replicas. Peers and clients find them by name. A replacement with a random name and an empty disk would break both.

**One PVC per pod:** The volumeClaimTemplate creates a separate PVC for each pod and ties it to the same-numbered pod. db-1's disk always goes back to db-1.

**Order on purpose:** Ordered creation and updates suit systems that must bootstrap in sequence, or should upgrade one member at a time.

**Mistakes are survivable:** Scale from three to one by accident, and the PVCs for db-1 and db-2 are still there when you scale back up. Deleting the StatefulSet leaves its PVCs in place too.

**The limit:** A StatefulSet manages identity and storage, not database logic. It cannot promote a replica, rebuild one or run backups.

quiz.q: Someone scales a three-pod database StatefulSet down to one by mistake, then back to three an hour later. What state are db-1 and db-2 in?
quiz.a: They return with their original PVCs, because scaling down does not delete PVCs by default. They reattach their old data; the database then only has to catch up on the missed hour.

mcq.q: A StatefulSet's db-1 pod is killed. What does its replacement get?
options: The name db-1 and the same PVC
A new random name and a fresh PVC
The name db-1 and a fresh empty PVC
The next free name, db-3, and db-1's PVC
mcq.why: StatefulSets keep stable names and bind each pod's PVC from the volumeClaimTemplate to the same-numbered pod, so db-1 reattaches its own disk.

hook: Your database primary dies on Kubernetes and the StatefulSet reacts. Which replica does it promote?

predict.q: A StatefulSet runs a three-replica database. The primary's node dies. What does the StatefulSet do?
options: Tries to bring back the same pod with the same volume
Promotes the most up-to-date replica to primary
Starts a fresh primary from the latest backup

title: A StatefulSet has never heard of your database
body:
A StatefulSet keeps names and disks stable, and that is all. It knows nothing about the database inside the pods. It will not promote a replica when the primary fails. It will not rebuild a lost replica or run backups. It will not do a safe rolling upgrade that waits for replication to catch up before touching the next pod.

It knows whether a pod is running. Whether that pod's data is current is invisible to it.
takeaway: Running is not the same as caught up.
deeper:
**The upgrade trap:** A rolling update restarts pods in order, but it moves on once a pod is running and ready, not once its data has caught up. If the replica inside has not caught up with the primary, restarting the next member can leave too few current copies.

**The failover trap:** When the primary's node dies, the StatefulSet tries to bring back the same pod with the same volume. For a zonal or local volume that can be slow or impossible, while a healthy replica sits idle.

**Out of scope entirely:** Backups, including consistency steps like checkpointing before a snapshot.

**Who fills the gap:** These were a DBA's jobs. On Kubernetes they must be automated, and the thing that automates them is an **operator**, a controller that encodes how one specific system fails over, rebuilds and upgrades. Before trusting one, ask whether it has been exercised under real failure.

quiz.q: During a cluster upgrade, all three database pods in a StatefulSet restart in order and report Running within minutes. Why is that not proof the upgrade was safe?
quiz.a: Running only means the process is up. The StatefulSet never checked replication, so members may have restarted before the previous one caught up, briefly leaving too few current copies.

mcq.q: What does a StatefulSet wait for before updating the next pod in a rolling update?
options: The previous pod to be running and ready
Replication lag to return to zero
A fresh backup to complete
The primary role to move elsewhere
mcq.why: A StatefulSet only sees pod state. Replication health, backups and role changes are database knowledge, which only an operator can supply.

hook: Kubernetes promises that a pod can run anywhere. Which storage choice quietly takes that promise away?
title: A local PV chains its pod to one node
body:
A **local PV** exposes a node's own disk, such as NVMe, as a PersistentVolume. You get local-NVMe speed, but the data lives in one machine, so the PV requires **node affinity**: its pod can only run on that node.

If the node fails, the pod cannot move and the data may be lost. Core Kubernetes cannot provision local PVs dynamically, and the docs recommend WaitForFirstConsumer for them. They make sense only when the application replicates its own data.
takeaway: Pin a pod to a disk, and the disk's fate becomes the pod's.
deeper:
**What you gain:** Local NVMe latency of tens of microseconds and very high IOPS, with no per-volume product cap.

**What you give up:**
1. Scheduling freedom. Node affinity pins the pod, so the scheduler cannot place it anywhere else.
2. Survival. Node replacement, planned or not, is data loss for that replica.
3. Convenience. With no dynamic provisioning in core Kubernetes, local PVs must be created ahead of time or by extra tooling.

**Why WaitForFirstConsumer:** The scheduler must weigh the pod's other constraints together with where free local disks exist before binding. Binding first could tie the pod to a node that cannot run it.

**The rule it inherits:** Use local storage only when the app replicates itself, so a lost node is just a replica to rebuild. Automation must notice that loss and start the rebuild, and you should know how long the rebuild takes.

quiz.q: A team puts a single-instance PostgreSQL on a local PV for speed. What happens the first time its node is replaced during a cluster upgrade?
quiz.a: The pod cannot move with its data, and the disk goes away with the node. With no replica anywhere else, the database's data is lost.

mcq.q: When is a Kubernetes local PV a reasonable home for a database?
options: When the database replicates its own data
When the node has spare NVMe capacity
When the StorageClass uses Immediate binding
When the reclaim policy is set to Retain
mcq.why: A local PV pins the pod to one node, so losing the node loses that copy. Only application-level replication makes that loss survivable.

hook: Somebody has to promote a replica when the primary dies at 3 a.m. On Kubernetes, who is that supposed to be?
title: Operators: the DBA's playbook, running as code
body:
Kubernetes keeps pods and disks alive, but it cannot run a database. Someone still has to bootstrap the cluster, add replicas, fail over, back up and upgrade. An **operator** is a controller that encodes that operational knowledge for one specific system.

It fills the gap StatefulSets leave. Where a StatefulSet sees only running pods, an operator understands the database inside. It can promote a replica when the primary dies, rebuild lost replicas and roll upgrades only as fast as replication health allows.
takeaway: Your operator's code is your on-call runbook. Test it like one.
deeper:
**How it works:** An operator reconciles actual state toward desired state, like any Kubernetes controller, but with domain logic. A resource might declare three replicas, a version and daily backups. The operator keeps acting until that is true.

**What it must handle on Kubernetes:**
1. Node drains: wait for replication health before allowing the next drain.
2. Stuck detaches: fail over to a replica rather than wait for the volume.
3. Local PV loss: detect the lost replica and rebuild it.
4. Backups: have the database checkpoint before a snapshot when you need application consistency.

**The real risk:** An operator is only as good as its behavior on a bad day. One nobody has exercised under failure is an untested disaster-recovery plan.

**Examples:** Rook runs Ceph clusters on Kubernetes. HubSpot built the first Vitess operator and ran it in production.

quiz.q: A team runs a replicated database with a StatefulSet and a PodDisruptionBudget, but no operator. Name two jobs humans still have to do.
quiz.a: Any two of: bootstrapping, promoting a replica when the primary fails, rebuilding a lost replica, running backups, and rolling upgrades that wait for replication health.

mcq.q: Which job belongs to a database operator rather than a StatefulSet?
options: Promoting a replica when the primary fails
Giving each pod a stable network name
Creating one PVC per pod from a template
Restarting pods in a fixed order
mcq.why: Stable names, per-pod PVCs and ordered restarts are StatefulSet features. Failover needs database knowledge, which is what an operator encodes.

hook: Ceph serves block, file and object storage, with many moving parts. Who runs it for you on Kubernetes?
title: Rook turns Ceph into three kinds of Kubernetes storage
body:
Running Ceph by hand means deploying, scaling and upgrading many moving parts. **Rook** automates that. It is a CNCF graduated operator for Ceph that automates deploying, configuring, scaling, upgrading and monitoring Ceph clusters on Kubernetes.

Once Ceph is running, other pods get three interfaces: block storage through **RBD**, file storage through CephFS, and object storage through RGW. Rook's Ceph operator was declared stable in December 2018.
takeaway: An operator can run a whole storage platform, not just one database.
deeper:
**Why Ceph needs an operator:** Ceph has many daemons, placement rules, failure handling and upgrade steps. Rook turns those procedures into automation, so a team manages Ceph as Kubernetes resources and lets the operator handle deployment, scaling and upgrades.

**What pods can claim:**
1. RBD block volumes, used much like cloud volumes.
2. CephFS shared filesystems, for ReadWriteMany needs.
3. RGW, an object interface.

**How volumes reach pods:** Ceph ships its own CSI driver, so its volumes plug into Kubernetes through the same standard interface as the EBS and GCE PD drivers.

**One cluster, three uses:** A single Ceph cluster, managed as Kubernetes resources, can serve database volumes, shared directories and object buckets at once. Rook's Ceph operator was declared stable in December 2018.

quiz.q: An on-prem Kubernetes team needs block volumes for databases, a shared filesystem for notebooks and an object store for artifacts. How can one Rook-managed Ceph cluster cover all three?
quiz.a: Ceph serves block through RBD, shared files through CephFS and objects through RGW. Rook deploys and operates that single Ceph cluster, and pods consume whichever interface they need.

mcq.q: Through which Ceph interface does Rook provide block storage to pods?
options: RBD
CephFS
RGW
NFS
mcq.why: RBD is Ceph's block device interface. CephFS provides shared files and RGW provides object storage.

hook: HubSpot wanted its MySQL on Kubernetes, but no Vitess operator existed yet. What did it do?
title: HubSpot built the first Vitess operator itself
body:
HubSpot adopted Vitess, the MySQL sharding and management system, on Kubernetes from mid-2016. A 2019 CNCF case study says HubSpot built the first **Vitess operator** and had run it in production for about two years. Its engineers said Vitess let them unify data storage and microservices infrastructure on Kubernetes.

By 2023, HubSpot reported over a thousand MySQL clusters per environment on Vitess.

stat.label: MySQL clusters per environment on Vitess

takeaway: Past a thousand clusters, the runbook has to be code.
deeper:
**Two worlds, one platform:** A common setup runs databases on dedicated VMs with separate tooling and applications on Kubernetes. HubSpot's engineers said Vitess let them unify data storage and microservices infrastructure on Kubernetes instead.

**The timeline:**
1. Mid-2016: HubSpot adopts Vitess on Kubernetes.
2. 2019: a CNCF case study says it built the first Vitess operator and had run it in production for about two years.
3. 2023: HubSpot reports over a thousand MySQL clusters per environment on Vitess.

**Read the number carefully:** The 2023 figure counts MySQL clusters on Vitess. It does not say every one of them runs through the Kubernetes operator.

**Why Vitess fits:** Vitess replicates at the database layer, so durability does not have to live in any single disk. PlanetScale later ran Vitess on local NVMe with PlanetScale Metal, relying on that database replication for durability.

quiz.q: A colleague cites HubSpot as proof that a thousand MySQL clusters run through one Kubernetes operator. What does the record actually support?
quiz.a: HubSpot built the first Vitess operator and had run it about two years by 2019, and reported over a thousand MySQL clusters per environment on Vitess by 2023. It never says all use the operator.

mcq.q: What did a 2019 CNCF case study credit HubSpot with?
options: Building the first Vitess operator
Creating the Vitess sharding system
Writing the CSI storage standard
Launching the Rook Ceph operator
mcq.why: The case study says HubSpot built the first Vitess operator and had run it in production for about two years.

hook: A routine Kubernetes upgrade is a non-event for web pods. For a database, every node it drains becomes what?
title: To a database, every node drain is a failover
body:
A cluster upgrade drains nodes one by one. Stateless pods restart elsewhere and nobody notices. For a database, evicting the primary is a **failover**, and evicting replicas cuts redundancy. Use **PodDisruptionBudgets** so no more than one replica is down at a time, and have the operator wait for replication health before the next drain.

Zones add a harder limit. An EBS volume cannot move to another AZ, so when a zone fails, pods whose PVCs live there cannot reschedule anywhere else.
takeaway: Kubernetes can move a pod in seconds. It cannot move a zonal disk at all.
deeper:
**How drains go wrong:** If an upgrade drains nodes faster than replicas resync, several members can be down or behind at once. A PodDisruptionBudget sets how many pods must stay available and blocks voluntary evictions that would break it. The operator adds the database-aware part: confirm the restarted replica has caught up before the next drain proceeds.

**Why zones are harder:** EBS replicates only inside one AZ. A zone outage strands every pod whose data lives there. Kubernetes can reschedule the pod, but not its volume.

**The only defense:** Replicate across zones at the application level, so replicas in surviving zones take over. On AWS, cross-AZ durability is the application's job, or a managed database's.

**A quick check:** For each database, ask what happens if one node drains right now, and what happens if the whole zone holding its primary disappears.

quiz.q: A three-replica database on AWS keeps all replicas in one AZ for low latency, each on its own EBS volume. The AZ goes down. Why can't Kubernetes recover it by rescheduling?
quiz.a: Every PVC's EBS volume lives in that AZ and cannot move. Pods can be rescheduled to other zones, but their data cannot follow, so no replica survives outside the failed zone.

mcq.q: What does a PodDisruptionBudget do during a cluster upgrade?
options: Blocks evictions that would leave too few pods available
Checks replication lag before each node is drained
Moves zonal volumes to nodes in healthy zones
Pauses the upgrade until backups have completed
mcq.why: A PDB limits voluntary evictions to keep a minimum of pods up. Checking replication health is the operator's job, and zonal volumes cannot move.

hook: The primary's node dropped off the network, and its disk is fine. So why can the new pod wait for minutes?

predict.q: A database primary's node goes unreachable and its volume detach hangs. What is usually the fastest way back?
options: Promote an existing replica
Wait for the volume to detach and reattach
Restore a primary from the latest snapshot

title: A stuck detach can block your database for minutes
body:
Moving a network volume to a new node takes time. When the old node is unreachable rather than cleanly dead, the detach can get stuck and block the new pod for minutes. For a primary, those minutes are an outage. Operators should **fail over** to a replica instead of waiting for the volume.

Local disks fail differently. With a **local PV**, replacing a node is data loss for that replica. Automation must detect it and rebuild, without waiting for a human.
takeaway: Fail over to data that is already attached. Don't wait for a disk to travel.
deeper:
**Why detaches stick:** The system must be sure the old node has stopped writing before attaching the volume elsewhere. An unreachable node gives no such guarantee, so the system may wait before forcing the detach.

**The better move:** Promote an existing replica. Its data is already attached and current. Deal with the old volume later. Reattaching a network volume usually takes minutes, but not always, so replicas stay the fastest failover path.

**The silent failure:** A node replaced during an upgrade, or a hardware fault, removes a local replica's data. If nothing notices, the cluster runs with one fewer copy indefinitely.

**How long the gap lasts:** Rebuild time is data size divided by allowed bandwidth. A 10 TB replica rebuilt at 1.25 GB/s, 40% of a 25 Gbps link, takes about 2.2 hours of reduced redundancy.

quiz.q: After a node replacement, a database replica on a local PV comes back with an empty disk, and nobody is paged. What is the risk, and what should automation do?
quiz.a: The cluster silently runs with one fewer copy, so another failure could lose data. Automation should detect the lost replica and rebuild it from its peers right away.

mcq.q: Why can a volume detach get stuck when a node fails?
options: The old node is unreachable, not confirmed dead
The volume is still being snapshotted
The claim uses the Retain reclaim policy
The new node sits in a different zone
mcq.why: Before reattaching, the system must know the old node stopped writing. An unreachable node can't confirm that, so the detach may wait before being forced.

hook: One kubectl command, typed in the wrong context, can take production database disks with it. Which one?
title: One delete namespace can take the cloud disks too
body:
Kubernetes deletion cascades. A single `kubectl delete namespace` can remove every PVC in it, and under a `Delete` reclaim policy the cloud volumes go too. Defend in layers: `Retain`, deletion protection and off-cluster backups.

The other risk is quieter. Pods on the same node share its network bandwidth to EBS and the instance's EBS limits, so one heavy pod can slow a database next to it. Put heavy databases on **dedicated node pools**.
takeaway: A backup inside the blast radius is not a backup.
deeper:
**Why three layers:**
1. `Retain` stops the cascade at the volume.
2. Deletion protection guards the resources themselves.
3. Off-cluster backups survive even if something inside the cluster or account is destroyed.

Backups that live only in the same cluster can vanish in the same mistake.

**Noisy neighbors, again:** EBS spent years fighting noisy neighbors inside its storage fleet. The problem returns one level up. Each instance has limited bandwidth to EBS, and every pod on the node competes for it. A batch job doing heavy I/O can push up a database's latency.

**The fix:** Dedicated node pools, groups of nodes reserved for databases, give heavy databases the instance's EBS bandwidth to themselves and more predictable performance.

**The pattern:** Both risks come from Kubernetes treating pods as disposable and interchangeable. Stateful workloads need guardrails stateless apps never did.

quiz.q: A database shares nodes with a nightly batch job. Its p99 latency spikes every night, though its own volume is far below its IOPS limit. Likely cause and fix?
quiz.a: Pods on a node share its network bandwidth to EBS and the instance's EBS limits, so the batch job starves the database. Move the database to a dedicated node pool.

mcq.q: Why are off-cluster backups needed even with a Retain reclaim policy?
options: Retain only stops claim deletion from removing volumes
Retain volumes are deleted after a grace period
Retain disables snapshots of the volume
Retain keeps the metadata but discards the data
mcq.why: Retain guards one cascade. Mistakes that reach the cluster or account can still destroy in-cluster volumes and snapshots, so a copy must live outside.

hook: Can Kubernetes run databases? In a design review, that's the wrong question. What's the right one?
title: The question isn't whether Kubernetes can run databases
body:
Kubernetes can run databases. That was never the hard part. The real question is whether your team has an **operator** it trusts to fail over, rebuild and upgrade, and whether it has practiced those under real failure.

Many companies answer by splitting the fleet. Their largest stores go to managed databases or dedicated VMs. Kubernetes gets the long tail, where standard automation matters more than squeezing out latency.
takeaway: An operator you've never watched fail over is a hope, not a plan.
deeper:
**Where safety really lives:** Kubernetes supplies the parts: PVCs, StorageClasses, CSI, StatefulSets. Whether a database survives depends on the operator during the bad moments: a node drained mid-upgrade, a stuck detach, a lost local disk, a zone outage.

**What practice means:** Inject those failures on purpose. Check that failover, rebuild and upgrade do what you expect before a real incident tests them for you.

**Why the split:** The largest, most latency-critical stores justify dedicated infrastructure or a managed service, where latency can be tuned and specialists watch a few systems. A long tail of many smaller databases gains most from standardized automation, because hand care for each one does not scale.

**Questions to ask:** Which operator runs this database? When did it last fail over under real conditions? Who takes over if it misbehaves?

quiz.q: Your team wants to move its largest, most latency-sensitive database onto Kubernetes, using an operator nobody has tested in a failure. What should a senior reviewer ask first?
quiz.a: Whether the team trusts that operator to fail over, rebuild and upgrade, and has practiced those under real failure. If not, a managed database or dedicated VMs may be the safer home.

mcq.q: Which databases do many companies choose to run on Kubernetes?
options: The long tail of smaller databases
Their largest, most latency-critical stores
Only databases that have no replicas
Only read replicas of managed databases
mcq.why: The largest stores often go to managed databases or dedicated VMs. The long tail benefits most from Kubernetes' standard automation.

hook: Many machines need one shared home directory. A disk won't share and a bucket isn't a filesystem. What fits?
title: EFS, Filestore, Azure Files: one filesystem, many machines
body:
Shared home directories, content management, ML notebooks and legacy apps all want one POSIX filesystem that many machines mount at once. A block volume normally attaches to one machine, and object storage is not POSIX.

Clouds sell **managed network filesystems** for this. Amazon EFS speaks NFSv4.1, grows capacity elastically, and stores data across multiple AZs in its regional classes. Google Filestore is managed NFS for Compute Engine and GKE. Azure Files offers SMB and NFS shares. They usually back Kubernetes **ReadWriteMany** volumes.
takeaway: A block device has one owner. A shared filesystem has many.
deeper:
**Why block and objects fall short:** A block device has no coordination between writers, so a volume normally attaches to one machine at a time. Object storage lacks POSIX semantics such as in-place edits, directories and file locking that legacy software expects.

**What each service adds:**
1. EFS: NFSv4.1, capacity that grows automatically, and data across multiple AZs in regional classes, unlike single-AZ EBS.
2. Filestore: managed NFS for Compute Engine VMs and GKE.
3. Azure Files: SMB, common for Windows workloads, plus NFS.

**In Kubernetes:** A ReadWriteMany claim, mountable read-write by many nodes, is usually satisfied by one of these services. That is why they sit behind notebook and shared-content platforms.

**The catch:** Keeping POSIX consistent across many clients makes metadata operations slow, which limits where these filesystems belong.

quiz.q: Ten pods on different nodes must all write to the same directory of user uploads. Why won't an ordinary gp3 PVC work, and what backs the claim instead?
quiz.a: A gp3 volume is ReadWriteOnce: it attaches read-write to one node. A ReadWriteMany claim backed by a managed network filesystem such as EFS lets every node mount it.

mcq.q: Which AWS storage keeps data across multiple AZs in its regional classes?
options: Amazon EFS
Amazon EBS gp3
EC2 instance store
Amazon EBS io2
mcq.why: EFS regional classes spread data across AZs. EBS volumes replicate inside one AZ, and instance store is ephemeral local disk.

hook: On a shared network filesystem, a job over millions of tiny files crawls. The bytes aren't the issue. What is?
title: Millions of tiny files crawl on a shared filesystem
body:
A network filesystem must keep POSIX semantics consistent across many clients. That makes metadata operations such as `open`, `stat` and small-file creates much slower than on a local disk. A job touching millions of tiny files pays that cost millions of times.

So these filesystems are a poor fit for databases and tiny-file workloads. Large-scale analytics belongs on **object storage**, databases belong on **block storage**, and shared filesystems belong to genuinely shared files.
takeaway: Shared semantics cost a round trip. Don't pay it on every file.
deeper:
**Where the time goes:** On a local disk, opening or statting a file is a quick operation inside the kernel. On a network filesystem, the server must keep every client's view consistent, so metadata operations typically need network round trips and server-side coordination. Each one adds latency.

**Why databases lose:** A database needs fast, predictable random I/O and reliable fsync. Only one database instance should write its files anyway, so the sharing buys nothing and the network and protocol overhead is pure cost.

**Why analytics goes elsewhere:** Object storage scales throughput for huge datasets and skips POSIX metadata costs.

**The map:**
1. Immutable bulk data and analytics: objects.
2. Databases: block volumes, network or local.
3. Many machines needing the same POSIX tree, such as home directories, notebooks or legacy apps: shared filesystems.

quiz.q: A team puts PostgreSQL's data directory on EFS so any node can start the database. What do they pay, and what do they gain?
quiz.a: They pay network and protocol overhead on every I/O and fsync, plus slow metadata operations. They gain little, since only one PostgreSQL instance should write those files. Block storage fits better.

mcq.q: Which operations suffer most on a shared network filesystem compared with a local disk?
options: Metadata operations like open, stat and small creates
Large sequential reads of a single big file
Bulk uploads of immutable objects by key
Streaming appends to one already-open file
mcq.why: Keeping POSIX consistent across clients means metadata operations need coordination and round trips, so open, stat and small-file creates are much slower.

hook: Kafka says durability doesn't need fsync. PostgreSQL crashes itself when fsync fails. Can both be right?

predict.q: What does Kafka's documentation recommend for application-level fsync?
options: Leave it off and rely on replication
fsync after every message
fsync once per second

title: Kafka skips fsync, PostgreSQL panics on it: both right
body:
Kafka's documentation says durability does not require syncing data to disk, and recommends leaving application fsync off. PostgreSQL treats an fsync failure as fatal. Both are correct, because durability lives in different layers.

Kafka relies on **replication**: a failed broker recovers its data from other replicas. PostgreSQL relies on its local **write-ahead log** being on disk for committed transactions. After an fsync error the kernel may have dropped dirty pages, so the only safe move is to crash and recover from the WAL.
takeaway: Ask where durability lives before judging how a system treats fsync.
deeper:
**Where durability lives:** Kafka puts it in replication. PostgreSQL puts it in local storage. Each design follows consistently from that choice. Put durability in exactly one layer, on purpose.

**What it means for hardware:** Because Kafka's durability does not depend on one disk, it fits local NVMe well. A single-node PostgreSQL with no replica needs durable network volumes and snapshots. A replicated MySQL fleet can go local, as PlanetScale Metal did, with durability from database replication.

**The fsync mechanics:**
1. `write()` only copies data into the page cache.
2. `fsync()` forces dirty pages and metadata to stable storage and waits.
3. On Linux, a failed background write-back can mark pages clean and drop the data.
4. A later fsync from another process may not report the error.

**Why retrying fails:** After an fsync error, you cannot trust the page cache.

quiz.q: A team runs a single-node PostgreSQL on local NVMe and disables fsync, reasoning that Kafka does fine without it. Why is that wrong?
quiz.a: Kafka's durability comes from replicas on other brokers. A single PostgreSQL node has no replica, so committed data exists only in its local WAL; without fsync, a power loss can erase it.

mcq.q: What does PostgreSQL do after an fsync failure?
options: Panic and recover from the WAL
Retry the fsync until it succeeds
Mark the pages dirty and rewrite them
Switch the file to direct I/O mode
mcq.why: The kernel may have dropped the dirty pages and the error may not be reported again, so a retry can falsely succeed. Replaying the WAL is the safe path.
